Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verse 1–7 (part 1 of 2):

It is narrated that its letters are fourteen thousand, five hundred and twenty-five letters, three thousand, four hundred and eighty words, and two hundred verses.

Its virtues:

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned on Friday, Allah sends blessings upon him, and so do His angels, until the sun sets." [1] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/168.]]

Zurr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah of Al 'Imran will be given, for every verse in it, a safeguard upon the bridge of Hell (Jahannam)." [2] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/232.]]

Abu Ishaq narrated from Sulaym ibn Handhala, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever recites Al 'Imran is wealthy."

Yahya ibn Na'im, from his father, from Abu al-Mu'arrij, from 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Learn al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they are the two luminous ones (al-Zahrawan), and they will come on the Day of Resurrection in the form of two clouds or two shades or two flocks of birds, pleading for their reciter until they admit him into Paradise." [3] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/361; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/159, with some variation in the hadith.]]

Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Abu al-Hurayn, from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Shami, who said: "Whoever recites the surah of al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran on the night of Friday, he will be given on the Day of Resurrection two wings with which he will fly over the Sirat." [4] [[Mizan al-I'tidal: 2/424, where it says: two wings strung with pearls and rubies.]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Zubayr, and Muhammad ibn Marwan from al-Kalbi, and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far al-Razi from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: This was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran. They were sixty riders who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and among them were fourteen men of their nobles. Among the fourteen were three men to whom their affairs returned: al-'Aqib, who was their commander and the one who advised them, and whose opinion they never departed from, and his name was 'Abd al-Masih; and al-Sayyid [their scholar] and the owner of their caravan, whose name was [al-Ayham, also said: Shurahbil]; and Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah, who was considered their rabbi (scholar), their leader, and the head of their schools. He had been honored among them and had taught their priests because of the goodness of his work in their religion, and the kings of Rome had honored him [and enriched him and built for him] churches, because of his knowledge and diligence.

So they came to the Messenger of Allah in Madinah and entered his mosque, after he had prayed the 'Asr, wearing striped Yemeni garments and cloaks fastened with clasps, in the finery of men of Bali al-Harith [for ease of pronunciation; originally: Banu al-Harith] ibn Ka'b. Some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who saw them said: "We have never seen a delegation like them!" Their prayer time came, so they stood and prayed in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they prayed facing the east.

The sayyid and the 'aqib spoke with the Messenger of Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Submit (aslimu)." They said: "We submitted before you." He said: "You lie. What prevents you from Islam is your claim [in the manuscript: your supplication] that Allah has a son, your worship of the cross, and your eating of pork." They said: "If Allah has no son, then whose son is He?" And they disputed with him all together concerning 'Isa (peace be upon him). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: [There is no child except that it resembles its father. They said: Yes. He said: Do you not] know that our Lord is living and does not die, while 'Isa will come to extinction? They said: Yes. He said: Do you not know that our Lord is the Sustainer of everything, who protects it and provides for it? They said: Yes. He said: Does 'Isa possess any of that? They said: No. He said: Do you not know that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah? They said: Yes. He said: Does 'Isa know any of that except what he was taught? They said: No. He said: Indeed our Lord fashioned 'Isa in the womb as He willed, and our Lord does not eat, drink, or excrete? They said: Yes. He said: Do you not know that 'Isa's mother carried him as a woman carries, then bore him as a woman bears her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, and he ate, drank, and excreted? They said: Yes. He said: Then how can this be as you claim? So they fell silent.

Then Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them the beginning of the surah of Al 'Imran, up to some eighty verses of it.

He, the Mighty, the Majestic, said: Alif Lam Mim.

Ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Qa'qa' al-Madani recited ' Alif Lam Mim' separated, and likewise all the disjointed letters with which surahs begin.

Ibn Ja'far al-Rawwasi, al-A'mash and al-Harami recited "Alif Lam Mim. Allah" with a cut (qat'), while the rest read it connected (wasl), with the mim fathah. As for the one who pronounces the mim with fathah and connects, there are two explanations:

The Basrans said: Because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (sakinayn), the vowel was moved to the lightest vowel.

The Kufans said: It was originally unvocalized, because the letters of the alphabet are built on pausal form (waqf). When the hamzat al-wasl came upon it, the alif was elided and the letter was pronounced continuously, so its vowel, the fathah, was transferred to the mim.

As for the one who cuts (qat'), he has two explanations:

The first: intending a pause, then cutting the hamzah for beginning, like the words of the poet:
"You will surely hear soon in their abodes: Allah is greatest, O vengeance for 'Uthman!"
[[al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 7/219; Taj al-'Arus: 3/70.]]

The second: that he treats it according to the dialect of those who pronounce the hamzat al-wasl as a full hamzah.
Like the words of the poet:
"When one exceeds two, it is revealed; and it is a daughter, and the multiplying of slanderers is worthy of it." [[al-Sihah: 1/294.]]

As for the one who separates and cuts, it is for magnification and exaltation: "Allah" is a beginning, and what follows is its predicate. "There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer" is its description. "He has sent down upon you the Book": Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla recited "nazala" with a light zay, and "al-kitab" with a raised ba'; the rest read it with a shadda on the zay and a fathah on the ba', for multiplicity, because the Qur'an was revealed in stages, piece by piece, and tanzil occurs repeatedly. He said: "And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel," because those two were revealed all at once. "He has sent down upon you, O Muhammad, the Book," the Qur'an, "with truth," with justice and sincerity. "Confirming": agreeing with "what lies between its hands," that is, what came before it of the scriptures, in matters of monotheism, prophethood, reports, and some legislation.

"And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel." The Basrans said: its origin is "wawriyah," from dawalah and harqalah. The first waw was changed into a ta', and the open ya' was made an alif, so it became "tawrah," then it was written with a ya' according to the root of the word. The Kufans said: it is "taf'alah," and the reason for it is what we have mentioned, like "tawsiyah" and "tawfiyah," so the ya' was changed into an alif, as the Tayy tribe does, saying to a girl "jaraah," and to a forelock "nasah." Its root comes from the saying "warra al-zand" when its fire is brought out, and I have transformed it. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: "Have you seen the fire that you kindle?" [[Surah al-Waqi'ah: 71.]] and He said: "By the sparking horses, striking sparks" [[Surah al-'Adiyat: 2.]]. It is called "tawrah" because it is light and radiance, indicated by His saying: "And a radiance and a reminder for the God-fearing" [[Surah al-Anbiya': 48.]]. This was said by al-Farra' and most scholars. [Al-Mu'arrij] said: it is from "tawriyah," which is concealing a thing and alluding to something else.

From the hadith: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "when he intended something, he concealed it by means of something else" [5].

Most tawriyah is by allusion and hinting, without clarity and explicit statement. It was also said: in Hebrew it is "nurwatho," meaning: the Law.

"Injil" is better than "najl," which is emergence, and from it a child is called "najl" because of its coming out.

Al-A'sha said:
"He was a noble son in the times his parents bore him, since they bore him, and what a good thing they bore."
[[al-Sihah: 1/222.]]

It was named thus because Allah the Exalted brought out through it what had been effaced of the truth, restoring it. It is also said that it is from "al-mutanajjal," which is breadth of the earth; one says: "I cut it wide (najlan)," meaning broad. It was named thus because it is a source which He brought out for them and widened for them as light and radiance. It was also said: in Syriac it is "anqlyun," meaning: the Law.

Al-Hasan read "al-Anjil" with a fathah on the hamzah; the rest read it with a kasrah, like "al-Iklil."

"From before" is raised as a termination (ghayah), and the termination here is the cutting off of the Book from it, like His saying: "To Allah belongs the command, from before and from after" [Surah al-Rum: 4]. And Zuhayr said:
"Whatever good they performed, it was only inherited by the fathers of their fathers before."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/173.]]

"A guidance for the people": a guide for whoever follows it, and it did not end, because it is a verbal noun, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state and a cut-off.

"And He sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan)": the distinction between truth and falsehood. Al-Suddi said: there is inversion and displacement in the verse; its meaning is: "And He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, and the Criterion as guidance for the God-fearing."

"Indeed those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah, for them is a severe punishment, and Allah is Mighty, Owner of retribution."

"Indeed nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah. He is the One who fashions you in the wombs as He wills: male and female, short and tall, black and white, handsome and ugly, happy and wretched."

"There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise."

"He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), perfected, clear, and detailed."

"They are the Mother of the Book," meaning: its origin, upon which rulings are based; it gathers the lawful and the unlawful, and it is set aside for the people of Islam. And they are the verses of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an, and in every book that the people of every religion accept, and about which the people of every land do not differ.

The Arabs call everything excellent and comprehensive, which serves as a reference for a people, by such names: as the Preserved Tablet is called "Mother of the Book," al-Fatihah "Mother of the Qur'an," Makkah "Mother of the Towns," the brain "Mother of the Head," the mother "umm," the banner "umm," the man who manages the affairs of the household "umm," and the cow, camel, or sheep by which the people of a house live "umm." 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to say to water: "This is my father," and to bread: "This is my mother," because the sustenance of bodies depends on them.

He said "Mother of the Book" and did not say "mothers of the books," because all the verses, in their completeness and unity, are like a single verse, and the speech of Allah is one.

It was also said: its meaning is a single word; so "they are the Mother of the Book," as He said: "And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign" [Surah al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning each of them is a sign.

"And others (akhar)": the plural of "ukhra." It is not declined because it is a derivative of "awakhir," like "Umar" and "Zufar." This is what al-Kisa'i said.

It was also said: its "akhar" was left undeclined because it is an adjective, like "jam'" and "kas'," which are not declined because they are adjectives.

It was also said: because it is built on "wahidah" in not taking tanwin, and another "wahidah" is undeclined.

"Mutashabihat": they resemble one another. The scholars differed concerning the muhkam and the mutashabih. Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi said: "The muhkam is the abrogating (nasikh) by which one acts." "The mutashabih is the abrogated (mansukh) which is believed in but not acted upon; this is a report from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas."

'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from him, saying: "The muhkamat of the Qur'an are the abrogating, its lawful and unlawful, its limits, its obligations, and what is commanded and acted upon."

And the mutashabihat: its abrogated, its preceding and succeeding, its parables, its oaths, and what is believed in but not acted upon.

Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiyah, from Abu Ishaq, said: Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His saying, "Among them are verses that are muhkamat": they are the three verses in Surah al-An'am, "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you..." [Surah al-An'am: 151] up to the end of the three verses; its counterpart in Surah al-Isra' is "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him..." [Surah al-Isra': 23] and the verses.

Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: "The muhkam is what contains the lawful and the unlawful, and whatever is other than that is mutashabih, [confirming] one another."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The muhkam is that which does not admit of more than one interpretation. The mutashabih is that which admits of several interpretations.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: Among the muhkam is what Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book of the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them), explained and made clear for Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, such as the story of Nuh, mentioned in twenty-four verses; the story of Hud in ten verses; the story of Salih in eight verses; the story of Ibrahim in eight verses; the story of Lut in eight verses; the story of Shu'ayb in ten verses; and the story of Musa in many verses.

And [the verses of] the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are mentioned in twenty-four verses.

The mutashabih is what the wording differs in their stories when repeated, as He said in one place concerning the story of Nuh: "We said: Carry in it..." [Surah Hud: 40], and in another place: "So load in it..." [Surah al-Mu'minun: 27].

And concerning the staff of Musa He said: "Then behold, it was a snake moving swiftly" [Surah Ta-Ha: 20], and in another place He said: "a manifest serpent" [Surah al-A'raf: 107], and similar.

Some of them said: "The muhkam is what the scholars know its interpretation and understand its meaning."

"The mutashabih is what no one has a way to know, of what Allah has kept to Himself knowledge of," such as the report of the time of the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, the rising of the sun from the west, the establishment of the Hour, and the passing away and ending of the world.

Abu Fakhitah said: "The muhkamat, which are the Mother of the Book, are the openings of the surahs, from which the Qur'an is extracted. Alif Lam Mim. 'That is the Book, there is no doubt in it' [Surah al-Baqarah: 1-2]: from it al-Baqarah was extracted; and 'Alif Lam Mim. Allah' [Surah Al 'Imran: 1-2]: from it Al 'Imran was extracted."

Ibn Kaysan said: "The muhkamat have clear proofs and manifest indications; whoever hears them has no need to seek their meanings in the mutashabih, whose knowledge is doubtful; by reflecting on it, the common people recognize the detail of the truth in it from falsehood."

Some of them said: "The muhkam is what there is consensus upon its interpretation, and the mutashabih is what its meaning is not clear."

Abu 'Uthman said: The muhkam is the Opening of the Book (Fatihat al-Kitab).

Al-Sha'bi said: I saw in some tafsirs [see Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/242, from the tafsir of al-Mawardi, and Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/10] that the mutashabih is [what its wording is obscure, while the muhkam is what its wording is clear; and on this basis the whole Qur'an is] muhkam from one aspect in meaning [with strength] [.....] [an illegible word], as Allah said: "A Book whose verses have been made precise" [Surah Hud: 1].

And the mutashabih from one aspect is that it resembles one part of it another in beauty and confirms one another.

Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Shadhan, said: The mutashabih is the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs. That is because the rulers of the Jews, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and their like, came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Huyayy said to him: "It has reached us that 'Alif Lam Mim' was revealed to you. Was it revealed to you?" He said: "Yes." Huyayy said: "If that is true, I know the lifespan of your community, which is seventy-one years. Has anything else been revealed to you?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Ra'" [Surah Yunus: 1]. Huyayy said: "This is greater than that; it is seventy-one and a hundred years. Has anything else been revealed?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Mim Sad" [Surah al-A'raf: 1]. He said: "This is greater than that; it is one hundred and sixty-one years. Has more been revealed?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Ra'" [Surah Hud? / Yunus]. He said: "This is more than a hundred and seventy years. You have confused us, and we do not know whether to take from its abundance or its little. We are among those who do not believe in this."

Then Allah the Exalted revealed: "He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are muhkamat, they are the Mother of the Book, and others that are mutashabihat. As for those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)": that is, a turning away from the truth. It was also said: doubt.

"They follow that which is mutashabih of it": the scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse.

Al-Rabi' said: They are the delegation of Najran, who disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not know that he is the Word of Allah and a Spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us," so Allah revealed this verse.

Al-Kalbi said: They are the Jews. [Ajhal] this Ummah in extracting it by the reckoning of the abjad. Ibn Jurayj said: They are the hypocrites.

[Al-Qa'ila] al-Hasan said: They are the Khawarij.

Qatadah, when he recited this verse, "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," said: "If they are not others, then they are the Sabaiyya, and I do not know who they are."

Some of them said: They are all the innovators (muhdathah).

Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu al-Walid Yazid ibn Abi Maytham and his father all narrated together from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book," and then he (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who ask about what is mutashabih of it and dispute concerning it, they are those whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has meant; so beware of them and do not associate with them." [6] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/9, with variation; Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 2/5, from several chains that vary.]]

"Seeking discord (ibtigha' al-fitnah)": seeking shirk, said al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Mujahid: seeking doubts and confusion, so that they may lead their ignorant astray by them.

**Ta'wil** (the interpretation or ultimate meaning) of it: its explanation and knowledge. The evidence is His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾ [18:78].

It was also said: the seeking of its outcome, and the seeking of the term of the lifespan of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, from the reckoning of the abjad (numerical value of letters). The evidence is His saying, ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wil)﴾ [4:59], meaning its outcome. Its origin is from the saying of the Arabs, "taawwala al-fata" (the young man reached his end), when he has reached maturity.

Al-A'sha said:

*"Because she was, [in her affection], taking the outcome of her love,*
*as the spring-born foal's mother took its outcome and it grew up."*

He means: this one (the male) became her gentle companion, so she submitted to him and sought him.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And none knows its interpretation (ta'wil) except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ [3:7]. The scholars differed concerning the structure of this verse and its ruling.

Some people said: the waw in His saying ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is the conjunctive waw (waw al-'atf). That is, the interpretation of the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses is known to God and known to those firmly rooted in knowledge, and they, along with their knowledge, say, ﴿We believe in it﴾.

This is the view of Mujahid, al-Rabi', Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and the one chosen by al-Qutaybi. They said: its meaning is that they know it and say ﴿We believe in it﴾; so His saying "they say" (yaqulluna) is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: those firmly rooted in knowledge, saying, "We believe in it."

Ibn al-Mufarragh al-Himyari said:

*"You have struck your love from its imam,*
*after days at Baram.*
*The wind weeps its grief,*
*and the lightning flashes in the cloud."*

He meant: "and the lightning flashes in its cloud, and weeps its grief too." If the lightning did not share the wind in weeping, there would be no sense in mentioning the lightning and its flashing.

The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿What God has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it belongs to God and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [59:7]. Then He said: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes﴾ [59:8], to the end of the verse.

Then He said: ﴿And those who settled the abode and the faith﴾ [59:9], meaning: and those who settled the abode. Then He said, ﴿And those who came after them﴾, and then He informed of them that they ﴿say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ [59:10], to the end of the verse.

There is no doubt that His saying ﴿And those who came after them﴾ is a conjunction with His saying ﴿and those who settled the abode﴾, and that they share with the poor emigrants and the Helpers in the fay (spoils), and that ﴿they say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ is among what is said by those ﴿who came after them﴾. So the meaning of the verse is: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, and while they deserve the fay, they ﴿say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ [59:10], that is, saying it as a circumstance. Likewise here, in ﴿they say, "Our Lord"﴾, that is, and they say, "We believe in it."

Among what supports this view is that God did not send down His Book except that its verses be pondered, and He mentions this to indicate the meaning He intended. He said: ﴿A blessed Book which We have sent down to you, that they may ponder its verses﴾ [38:29], and He said: ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾ [26:195].

*Mubin* means the manifest. And He said: ﴿with a Book We have detailed﴾ [7:52]. So He described all of it with detail and clarification, and He said: ﴿that you may clarify to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [16:44].

It is not permissible to clarify what is not known. And if it is permissible that the Messenger (ﷺ) knew it despite His saying "none knows it but God," then it is permissible that the godly scholars among his Companions know it.

He also said: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [7:3], and one is not commanded to follow what is not known. Moreover, if there were not this (knowledge) for those firmly rooted in knowledge, they would have no superiority over the teachers and the ignorant, since they too say, ﴿We believe in it; all is from our Lord﴾ [3:7]. Also, we have not seen any of the exegetes, to this extent, [a group] who abstain from anything of the tafsir (exegesis) of the Qur'an and say, "This is mutashabih, none knows it but God." Rather, they all explained it, even the letters of the alphabet and others.

Ibn 'Abbas used to say concerning this verse: "I am among those firmly rooted in knowledge."

Mujahid recited this verse and said: "I am among those who know its interpretation."

Samak narrated from Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I know the whole Qur'an except four: *ghislin*, *hanan*, *al-awwah*, and *al-tarqim*." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas at a certain time, and then he learned them later and explained them.

Others said: the waw in His saying ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is the waw of resumption (istinaf), and the speech is complete and ends at His saying ﴿and none knows its interpretation except God.﴾ Then it begins: ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all is from our Lord"﴾. So "those firmly rooted" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in "they say." This is the view of 'A'isha, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, the narration of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas, and the choice of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Mufaddal ibn Salama, and Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). They said: "Those firmly rooted do not know its interpretation, but they believe in it." The verse, according to this interpretation, refers to knowledge of what concerns the term of this community, the time of the establishment of the Hour, the end of the world, the time of the rising of the sun from its west, the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), the emergence of the Dajjal, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the knowledge of the spirit, and the like, which God has reserved for His own knowledge and which none of His creation has been informed of.

Some of them said: "Know that the mutashabih of the Book has been reserved by God for His knowledge apart from us, and we explain it, but we were not obligated to that. Rather, we were obliged to act upon His commands and avoid His prohibitions." What confirms this view is the reading of 'Abd Allah: "Its interpretation is known only to God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it.'"

And in a reading of [ ] (an unreadable word in the manuscript): "those firmly rooted in knowledge, we believe in it."

Its evidence also includes what is narrated from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, that he recited this verse and then said: "The knowledge of those firmly rooted in knowledge of the interpretation of the Qur'an ended at their saying, 'We believe in it; all is from our Lord.'"

Abu Nahik al-Asadi said: "You pause on this verse, and it is cut off." This view is more analogical in Arabic grammar and more fitting to the apparent features of the verse and its context, and God knows best.

*Al-rasikhun* (those firmly rooted): those who entered into knowledge, who perfected their knowledge and derived it, so that doubt does not enter into their understanding. Its origin is from the firmness (rusukh) of a thing in another thing, which is its stability and its settling. It is said: "faith took firm root (rasakha) in the heart of so-and-so," and he is firmly rooted (yarsukh) with firm rooting (rasakhan wa rusukhan). Likewise in everything. It is also said rasakha (as in rasikha). This is like saying maslukh and masluukh. The poet said:

*"Surely love for you has taken firm root in the heart,*
*for the Prophet; its verses refused to be changed."*

Some of the scholarly exegetes said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge are the believers among the People of the Book, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and [Ibn Suriya and Ka'b]."

It was said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge are some of those who studied the knowledge of the Torah."

It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik [and Abu al-Darda' and Abu Umama] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked, "Who are those firmly rooted in knowledge?" He said: "Those whose right hand is sincere (in deed), whose tongue is truthful, whose heart is upright, and who are chaste in belly and private parts; that is the one firmly rooted in knowledge."

Wuhayb said: "I heard Malik ibn Anas being asked about the interpretation of His saying, 'and those firmly rooted in knowledge,' who are they?" He said: "The scholar who acts upon what he knows is a follower of it."

Nafi' ibn Yazid said: "As if it is said, those firmly rooted in knowledge are the believers in God, who humble themselves in seeking His pleasure, who do not exalt themselves over those above them, nor [belittle] those beneath them."

Some of them said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge are those who find four things in their action: piety between themselves and God the Exalted, humility between themselves and the creation, asceticism between themselves and the world, and striving between themselves and their own selves."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said, concerning their saying, "We believe in it": God the Exalted named them "those firmly rooted in knowledge," and their being firmly rooted in knowledge is their saying, "We believe in it," that is, in the mutashabih; "all is from our Lord," the muhkam (clear) and the mutashabih, the abrogating (nasikh) and the abrogated (mansukh), what we know and what we do not know.

Al-Mubarrad said: "Some people claim that 'min 'indi' (from) here is superfluous (silah), and its meaning is: all is from our Lord."

*Wa ma yadhdhakkaru* (and none takes heed): is admonished by what is in the Qur'an.

*Illa ulu al-albab* (except the people of understanding): those possessing intellects. The *lubb* (kernel) of everything is its pure essence, [and therefore the intellect is called *lubb*].

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verse 1–7 (part 1 of 2):

It is narrated that its letters are fourteen thousand, five hundred and twenty-five letters, three thousand, four hundred and eighty words, and two hundred verses.

Its virtues:

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned on Friday, Allah sends blessings upon him, and so do His angels, until the sun sets." [1] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/168.]]

Zurr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah of Al 'Imran will be given, for every verse in it, a safeguard upon the bridge of Hell (Jahannam)." [2] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/232.]]

Abu Ishaq narrated from Sulaym ibn Handhala, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever recites Al 'Imran is wealthy."

Yahya ibn Na'im, from his father, from Abu al-Mu'arrij, from 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Learn al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they are the two luminous ones (al-Zahrawan), and they will come on the Day of Resurrection in the form of two clouds or two shades or two flocks of birds, pleading for their reciter until they admit him into Paradise." [3] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/361; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/159, with some variation in the hadith.]]

Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Abu al-Hurayn, from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Shami, who said: "Whoever recites the surah of al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran on the night of Friday, he will be given on the Day of Resurrection two wings with which he will fly over the Sirat." [4] [[Mizan al-I'tidal: 2/424, where it says: two wings strung with pearls and rubies.]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Zubayr, and Muhammad ibn Marwan from al-Kalbi, and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far al-Razi from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: This was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran. They were sixty riders who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and among them were fourteen men of their nobles. Among the fourteen were three men to whom their affairs returned: al-'Aqib, who was their commander and the one who advised them, and whose opinion they never departed from, and his name was 'Abd al-Masih; and al-Sayyid [their scholar] and the owner of their caravan, whose name was [al-Ayham, also said: Shurahbil]; and Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah, who was considered their rabbi (scholar), their leader, and the head of their schools. He had been honored among them and had taught their priests because of the goodness of his work in their religion, and the kings of Rome had honored him [and enriched him and built for him] churches, because of his knowledge and diligence.

So they came to the Messenger of Allah in Madinah and entered his mosque, after he had prayed the 'Asr, wearing striped Yemeni garments and cloaks fastened with clasps, in the finery of men of Bali al-Harith [for ease of pronunciation; originally: Banu al-Harith] ibn Ka'b. Some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who saw them said: "We have never seen a delegation like them!" Their prayer time came, so they stood and prayed in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they prayed facing the east.

The sayyid and the 'aqib spoke with the Messenger of Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Submit (aslimu)." They said: "We submitted before you." He said: "You lie. What prevents you from Islam is your claim [in the manuscript: your supplication] that Allah has a son, your worship of the cross, and your eating of pork." They said: "If Allah has no son, then whose son is He?" And they disputed with him all together concerning 'Isa (peace be upon him). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: [There is no child except that it resembles its father. They said: Yes. He said: Do you not] know that our Lord is living and does not die, while 'Isa will come to extinction? They said: Yes. He said: Do you not know that our Lord is the Sustainer of everything, who protects it and provides for it? They said: Yes. He said: Does 'Isa possess any of that? They said: No. He said: Do you not know that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah? They said: Yes. He said: Does 'Isa know any of that except what he was taught? They said: No. He said: Indeed our Lord fashioned 'Isa in the womb as He willed, and our Lord does not eat, drink, or excrete? They said: Yes. He said: Do you not know that 'Isa's mother carried him as a woman carries, then bore him as a woman bears her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, and he ate, drank, and excreted? They said: Yes. He said: Then how can this be as you claim? So they fell silent.

Then Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them the beginning of the surah of Al 'Imran, up to some eighty verses of it.

He, the Mighty, the Majestic, said: Alif Lam Mim.

Ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Qa'qa' al-Madani recited ' Alif Lam Mim' separated, and likewise all the disjointed letters with which surahs begin.

Ibn Ja'far al-Rawwasi, al-A'mash and al-Harami recited "Alif Lam Mim. Allah" with a cut (qat'), while the rest read it connected (wasl), with the mim fathah. As for the one who pronounces the mim with fathah and connects, there are two explanations:

The Basrans said: Because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (sakinayn), the vowel was moved to the lightest vowel.

The Kufans said: It was originally unvocalized, because the letters of the alphabet are built on pausal form (waqf). When the hamzat al-wasl came upon it, the alif was elided and the letter was pronounced continuously, so its vowel, the fathah, was transferred to the mim.

As for the one who cuts (qat'), he has two explanations:

The first: intending a pause, then cutting the hamzah for beginning, like the words of the poet:
"You will surely hear soon in their abodes: Allah is greatest, O vengeance for 'Uthman!"
[[al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 7/219; Taj al-'Arus: 3/70.]]

The second: that he treats it according to the dialect of those who pronounce the hamzat al-wasl as a full hamzah.
Like the words of the poet:
"When one exceeds two, it is revealed; and it is a daughter, and the multiplying of slanderers is worthy of it." [[al-Sihah: 1/294.]]

As for the one who separates and cuts, it is for magnification and exaltation: "Allah" is a beginning, and what follows is its predicate. "There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer" is its description. "He has sent down upon you the Book": Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla recited "nazala" with a light zay, and "al-kitab" with a raised ba'; the rest read it with a shadda on the zay and a fathah on the ba', for multiplicity, because the Qur'an was revealed in stages, piece by piece, and tanzil occurs repeatedly. He said: "And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel," because those two were revealed all at once. "He has sent down upon you, O Muhammad, the Book," the Qur'an, "with truth," with justice and sincerity. "Confirming": agreeing with "what lies between its hands," that is, what came before it of the scriptures, in matters of monotheism, prophethood, reports, and some legislation.

"And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel." The Basrans said: its origin is "wawriyah," from dawalah and harqalah. The first waw was changed into a ta', and the open ya' was made an alif, so it became "tawrah," then it was written with a ya' according to the root of the word. The Kufans said: it is "taf'alah," and the reason for it is what we have mentioned, like "tawsiyah" and "tawfiyah," so the ya' was changed into an alif, as the Tayy tribe does, saying to a girl "jaraah," and to a forelock "nasah." Its root comes from the saying "warra al-zand" when its fire is brought out, and I have transformed it. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: "Have you seen the fire that you kindle?" [[Surah al-Waqi'ah: 71.]] and He said: "By the sparking horses, striking sparks" [[Surah al-'Adiyat: 2.]]. It is called "tawrah" because it is light and radiance, indicated by His saying: "And a radiance and a reminder for the God-fearing" [[Surah al-Anbiya': 48.]]. This was said by al-Farra' and most scholars. [Al-Mu'arrij] said: it is from "tawriyah," which is concealing a thing and alluding to something else.

From the hadith: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "when he intended something, he concealed it by means of something else" [5].

Most tawriyah is by allusion and hinting, without clarity and explicit statement. It was also said: in Hebrew it is "nurwatho," meaning: the Law.

"Injil" is better than "najl," which is emergence, and from it a child is called "najl" because of its coming out.

Al-A'sha said:
"He was a noble son in the times his parents bore him, since they bore him, and what a good thing they bore."
[[al-Sihah: 1/222.]]

It was named thus because Allah the Exalted brought out through it what had been effaced of the truth, restoring it. It is also said that it is from "al-mutanajjal," which is breadth of the earth; one says: "I cut it wide (najlan)," meaning broad. It was named thus because it is a source which He brought out for them and widened for them as light and radiance. It was also said: in Syriac it is "anqlyun," meaning: the Law.

Al-Hasan read "al-Anjil" with a fathah on the hamzah; the rest read it with a kasrah, like "al-Iklil."

"From before" is raised as a termination (ghayah), and the termination here is the cutting off of the Book from it, like His saying: "To Allah belongs the command, from before and from after" [Surah al-Rum: 4]. And Zuhayr said:
"Whatever good they performed, it was only inherited by the fathers of their fathers before."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/173.]]

"A guidance for the people": a guide for whoever follows it, and it did not end, because it is a verbal noun, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state and a cut-off.

"And He sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan)": the distinction between truth and falsehood. Al-Suddi said: there is inversion and displacement in the verse; its meaning is: "And He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, and the Criterion as guidance for the God-fearing."

"Indeed those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah, for them is a severe punishment, and Allah is Mighty, Owner of retribution."

"Indeed nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah. He is the One who fashions you in the wombs as He wills: male and female, short and tall, black and white, handsome and ugly, happy and wretched."

"There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise."

"He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), perfected, clear, and detailed."

"They are the Mother of the Book," meaning: its origin, upon which rulings are based; it gathers the lawful and the unlawful, and it is set aside for the people of Islam. And they are the verses of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an, and in every book that the people of every religion accept, and about which the people of every land do not differ.

The Arabs call everything excellent and comprehensive, which serves as a reference for a people, by such names: as the Preserved Tablet is called "Mother of the Book," al-Fatihah "Mother of the Qur'an," Makkah "Mother of the Towns," the brain "Mother of the Head," the mother "umm," the banner "umm," the man who manages the affairs of the household "umm," and the cow, camel, or sheep by which the people of a house live "umm." 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to say to water: "This is my father," and to bread: "This is my mother," because the sustenance of bodies depends on them.

He said "Mother of the Book" and did not say "mothers of the books," because all the verses, in their completeness and unity, are like a single verse, and the speech of Allah is one.

It was also said: its meaning is a single word; so "they are the Mother of the Book," as He said: "And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign" [Surah al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning each of them is a sign.

"And others (akhar)": the plural of "ukhra." It is not declined because it is a derivative of "awakhir," like "Umar" and "Zufar." This is what al-Kisa'i said.

It was also said: its "akhar" was left undeclined because it is an adjective, like "jam'" and "kas'," which are not declined because they are adjectives.

It was also said: because it is built on "wahidah" in not taking tanwin, and another "wahidah" is undeclined.

"Mutashabihat": they resemble one another. The scholars differed concerning the muhkam and the mutashabih. Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi said: "The muhkam is the abrogating (nasikh) by which one acts." "The mutashabih is the abrogated (mansukh) which is believed in but not acted upon; this is a report from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas."

'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from him, saying: "The muhkamat of the Qur'an are the abrogating, its lawful and unlawful, its limits, its obligations, and what is commanded and acted upon."

And the mutashabihat: its abrogated, its preceding and succeeding, its parables, its oaths, and what is believed in but not acted upon.

Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiyah, from Abu Ishaq, said: Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His saying, "Among them are verses that are muhkamat": they are the three verses in Surah al-An'am, "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you..." [Surah al-An'am: 151] up to the end of the three verses; its counterpart in Surah al-Isra' is "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him..." [Surah al-Isra': 23] and the verses.

Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: "The muhkam is what contains the lawful and the unlawful, and whatever is other than that is mutashabih, [confirming] one another."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The muhkam is that which does not admit of more than one interpretation. The mutashabih is that which admits of several interpretations.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: Among the muhkam is what Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book of the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them), explained and made clear for Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, such as the story of Nuh, mentioned in twenty-four verses; the story of Hud in ten verses; the story of Salih in eight verses; the story of Ibrahim in eight verses; the story of Lut in eight verses; the story of Shu'ayb in ten verses; and the story of Musa in many verses.

And [the verses of] the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are mentioned in twenty-four verses.

The mutashabih is what the wording differs in their stories when repeated, as He said in one place concerning the story of Nuh: "We said: Carry in it..." [Surah Hud: 40], and in another place: "So load in it..." [Surah al-Mu'minun: 27].

And concerning the staff of Musa He said: "Then behold, it was a snake moving swiftly" [Surah Ta-Ha: 20], and in another place He said: "a manifest serpent" [Surah al-A'raf: 107], and similar.

Some of them said: "The muhkam is what the scholars know its interpretation and understand its meaning."

"The mutashabih is what no one has a way to know, of what Allah has kept to Himself knowledge of," such as the report of the time of the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, the rising of the sun from the west, the establishment of the Hour, and the passing away and ending of the world.

Abu Fakhitah said: "The muhkamat, which are the Mother of the Book, are the openings of the surahs, from which the Qur'an is extracted. Alif Lam Mim. 'That is the Book, there is no doubt in it' [Surah al-Baqarah: 1-2]: from it al-Baqarah was extracted; and 'Alif Lam Mim. Allah' [Surah Al 'Imran: 1-2]: from it Al 'Imran was extracted."

Ibn Kaysan said: "The muhkamat have clear proofs and manifest indications; whoever hears them has no need to seek their meanings in the mutashabih, whose knowledge is doubtful; by reflecting on it, the common people recognize the detail of the truth in it from falsehood."

Some of them said: "The muhkam is what there is consensus upon its interpretation, and the mutashabih is what its meaning is not clear."

Abu 'Uthman said: The muhkam is the Opening of the Book (Fatihat al-Kitab).

Al-Sha'bi said: I saw in some tafsirs [see Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/242, from the tafsir of al-Mawardi, and Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/10] that the mutashabih is [what its wording is obscure, while the muhkam is what its wording is clear; and on this basis the whole Qur'an is] muhkam from one aspect in meaning [with strength] [.....] [an illegible word], as Allah said: "A Book whose verses have been made precise" [Surah Hud: 1].

And the mutashabih from one aspect is that it resembles one part of it another in beauty and confirms one another.

Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Shadhan, said: The mutashabih is the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs. That is because the rulers of the Jews, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and their like, came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Huyayy said to him: "It has reached us that 'Alif Lam Mim' was revealed to you. Was it revealed to you?" He said: "Yes." Huyayy said: "If that is true, I know the lifespan of your community, which is seventy-one years. Has anything else been revealed to you?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Ra'" [Surah Yunus: 1]. Huyayy said: "This is greater than that; it is seventy-one and a hundred years. Has anything else been revealed?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Mim Sad" [Surah al-A'raf: 1]. He said: "This is greater than that; it is one hundred and sixty-one years. Has more been revealed?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Ra'" [Surah Hud? / Yunus]. He said: "This is more than a hundred and seventy years. You have confused us, and we do not know whether to take from its abundance or its little. We are among those who do not believe in this."

Then Allah the Exalted revealed: "He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are muhkamat, they are the Mother of the Book, and others that are mutashabihat. As for those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)": that is, a turning away from the truth. It was also said: doubt.

"They follow that which is mutashabih of it": the scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse.

Al-Rabi' said: They are the delegation of Najran, who disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not know that he is the Word of Allah and a Spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us," so Allah revealed this verse.

Al-Kalbi said: They are the Jews. [Ajhal] this Ummah in extracting it by the reckoning of the abjad. Ibn Jurayj said: They are the hypocrites.

[Al-Qa'ila] al-Hasan said: They are the Khawarij.

Qatadah, when he recited this verse, "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," said: "If they are not others, then they are the Sabaiyya, and I do not know who they are."

Some of them said: They are all the innovators (muhdathah).

Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu al-Walid Yazid ibn Abi Maytham and his father all narrated together from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book," and then he (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who ask about what is mutashabih of it and dispute concerning it, they are those whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has meant; so beware of them and do not associate with them." [6] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/9, with variation; Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 2/5, from several chains that vary.]]

"Seeking discord (ibtigha' al-fitnah)": seeking shirk, said al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Mujahid: seeking doubts and confusion, so that they may lead their ignorant astray by them.

**Ta'wil** (the interpretation or ultimate meaning) of it: its explanation and knowledge. The evidence is His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾ [18:78].

It was also said: the seeking of its outcome, and the seeking of the term of the lifespan of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, from the reckoning of the abjad (numerical value of letters). The evidence is His saying, ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wil)﴾ [4:59], meaning its outcome. Its origin is from the saying of the Arabs, "taawwala al-fata" (the young man reached his end), when he has reached maturity.

Al-A'sha said:

*"Because she was, [in her affection], taking the outcome of her love,*
*as the spring-born foal's mother took its outcome and it grew up."*

He means: this one (the male) became her gentle companion, so she submitted to him and sought him.

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And none knows its interpretation (ta'wil) except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ [3:7]. The scholars differed concerning the structure of this verse and its ruling.

Some people said: the waw in His saying ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is the conjunctive waw (waw al-'atf). That is, the interpretation of the ambiguous (mutashabih) verses is known to God and known to those firmly rooted in knowledge, and they, along with their knowledge, say, ﴿We believe in it﴾.

This is the view of Mujahid, al-Rabi', Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, and the one chosen by al-Qutaybi. They said: its meaning is that they know it and say ﴿We believe in it﴾; so His saying "they say" (yaqulluna) is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the meaning is: those firmly rooted in knowledge, saying, "We believe in it."

Ibn al-Mufarragh al-Himyari said:

*"You have struck your love from its imam,*
*after days at Baram.*
*The wind weeps its grief,*
*and the lightning flashes in the cloud."*

He meant: "and the lightning flashes in its cloud, and weeps its grief too." If the lightning did not share the wind in weeping, there would be no sense in mentioning the lightning and its flashing.

The evidence for this interpretation is His saying: ﴿What God has restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it belongs to God and to the Messenger, and to the near of kin, the orphans, the needy, and the wayfarer﴾ [59:7]. Then He said: ﴿For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes﴾ [59:8], to the end of the verse.

Then He said: ﴿And those who settled the abode and the faith﴾ [59:9], meaning: and those who settled the abode. Then He said, ﴿And those who came after them﴾, and then He informed of them that they ﴿say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ [59:10], to the end of the verse.

There is no doubt that His saying ﴿And those who came after them﴾ is a conjunction with His saying ﴿and those who settled the abode﴾, and that they share with the poor emigrants and the Helpers in the fay (spoils), and that ﴿they say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ is among what is said by those ﴿who came after them﴾. So the meaning of the verse is: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, and while they deserve the fay, they ﴿say, "Our Lord, forgive us"﴾ [59:10], that is, saying it as a circumstance. Likewise here, in ﴿they say, "Our Lord"﴾, that is, and they say, "We believe in it."

Among what supports this view is that God did not send down His Book except that its verses be pondered, and He mentions this to indicate the meaning He intended. He said: ﴿A blessed Book which We have sent down to you, that they may ponder its verses﴾ [38:29], and He said: ﴿in clear Arabic tongue﴾ [26:195].

*Mubin* means the manifest. And He said: ﴿with a Book We have detailed﴾ [7:52]. So He described all of it with detail and clarification, and He said: ﴿that you may clarify to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [16:44].

It is not permissible to clarify what is not known. And if it is permissible that the Messenger (ﷺ) knew it despite His saying "none knows it but God," then it is permissible that the godly scholars among his Companions know it.

He also said: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [7:3], and one is not commanded to follow what is not known. Moreover, if there were not this (knowledge) for those firmly rooted in knowledge, they would have no superiority over the teachers and the ignorant, since they too say, ﴿We believe in it; all is from our Lord﴾ [3:7]. Also, we have not seen any of the exegetes, to this extent, [a group] who abstain from anything of the tafsir (exegesis) of the Qur'an and say, "This is mutashabih, none knows it but God." Rather, they all explained it, even the letters of the alphabet and others.

Ibn 'Abbas used to say concerning this verse: "I am among those firmly rooted in knowledge."

Mujahid recited this verse and said: "I am among those who know its interpretation."

Samak narrated from Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "I know the whole Qur'an except four: *ghislin*, *hanan*, *al-awwah*, and *al-tarqim*." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas at a certain time, and then he learned them later and explained them.

Others said: the waw in His saying ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge﴾ is the waw of resumption (istinaf), and the speech is complete and ends at His saying ﴿and none knows its interpretation except God.﴾ Then it begins: ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all is from our Lord"﴾. So "those firmly rooted" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in "they say." This is the view of 'A'isha, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, the narration of Tawus from Ibn 'Abbas, and the choice of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Mufaddal ibn Salama, and Muhammad ibn Jarir (al-Tabari). They said: "Those firmly rooted do not know its interpretation, but they believe in it." The verse, according to this interpretation, refers to knowledge of what concerns the term of this community, the time of the establishment of the Hour, the end of the world, the time of the rising of the sun from its west, the descent of 'Isa (peace be upon him), the emergence of the Dajjal, Ya'juj and Ma'juj, the knowledge of the spirit, and the like, which God has reserved for His own knowledge and which none of His creation has been informed of.

Some of them said: "Know that the mutashabih of the Book has been reserved by God for His knowledge apart from us, and we explain it, but we were not obligated to that. Rather, we were obliged to act upon His commands and avoid His prohibitions." What confirms this view is the reading of 'Abd Allah: "Its interpretation is known only to God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it.'"

And in a reading of [ ] (an unreadable word in the manuscript): "those firmly rooted in knowledge, we believe in it."

Its evidence also includes what is narrated from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, that he recited this verse and then said: "The knowledge of those firmly rooted in knowledge of the interpretation of the Qur'an ended at their saying, 'We believe in it; all is from our Lord.'"

Abu Nahik al-Asadi said: "You pause on this verse, and it is cut off." This view is more analogical in Arabic grammar and more fitting to the apparent features of the verse and its context, and God knows best.

*Al-rasikhun* (those firmly rooted): those who entered into knowledge, who perfected their knowledge and derived it, so that doubt does not enter into their understanding. Its origin is from the firmness (rusukh) of a thing in another thing, which is its stability and its settling. It is said: "faith took firm root (rasakha) in the heart of so-and-so," and he is firmly rooted (yarsukh) with firm rooting (rasakhan wa rusukhan). Likewise in everything. It is also said rasakha (as in rasikha). This is like saying maslukh and masluukh. The poet said:

*"Surely love for you has taken firm root in the heart,*
*for the Prophet; its verses refused to be changed."*

Some of the scholarly exegetes said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge are the believers among the People of the Book, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and [Ibn Suriya and Ka'b]."

It was said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge are some of those who studied the knowledge of the Torah."

It is narrated from Anas ibn Malik [and Abu al-Darda' and Abu Umama] that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked, "Who are those firmly rooted in knowledge?" He said: "Those whose right hand is sincere (in deed), whose tongue is truthful, whose heart is upright, and who are chaste in belly and private parts; that is the one firmly rooted in knowledge."

Wuhayb said: "I heard Malik ibn Anas being asked about the interpretation of His saying, 'and those firmly rooted in knowledge,' who are they?" He said: "The scholar who acts upon what he knows is a follower of it."

Nafi' ibn Yazid said: "As if it is said, those firmly rooted in knowledge are the believers in God, who humble themselves in seeking His pleasure, who do not exalt themselves over those above them, nor [belittle] those beneath them."

Some of them said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge are those who find four things in their action: piety between themselves and God the Exalted, humility between themselves and the creation, asceticism between themselves and the world, and striving between themselves and their own selves."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Suddi said, concerning their saying, "We believe in it": God the Exalted named them "those firmly rooted in knowledge," and their being firmly rooted in knowledge is their saying, "We believe in it," that is, in the mutashabih; "all is from our Lord," the muhkam (clear) and the mutashabih, the abrogating (nasikh) and the abrogated (mansukh), what we know and what we do not know.

Al-Mubarrad said: "Some people claim that 'min 'indi' (from) here is superfluous (silah), and its meaning is: all is from our Lord."

*Wa ma yadhdhakkaru* (and none takes heed): is admonished by what is in the Qur'an.

*Illa ulu al-albab* (except the people of understanding): those possessing intellects. The *lubb* (kernel) of everything is its pure essence, [and therefore the intellect is called *lubb*].

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verse 1–7 (part 1 of 2):

It is narrated that its letters are fourteen thousand, five hundred and twenty-five letters, three thousand, four hundred and eighty words, and two hundred verses.

Its virtues:

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah in which Al 'Imran is mentioned on Friday, Allah sends blessings upon him, and so do His angels, until the sun sets." [1] [[Majma' al-Zawa'id: 2/168.]]

Zurr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the surah of Al 'Imran will be given, for every verse in it, a safeguard upon the bridge of Hell (Jahannam)." [2] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/232.]]

Abu Ishaq narrated from Sulaym ibn Handhala, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "Whoever recites Al 'Imran is wealthy."

Yahya ibn Na'im, from his father, from Abu al-Mu'arrij, from 'Umar, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Learn al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran, for they are the two luminous ones (al-Zahrawan), and they will come on the Day of Resurrection in the form of two clouds or two shades or two flocks of birds, pleading for their reciter until they admit him into Paradise." [3] [[Musnad Ahmad: 5/361; Majma' al-Zawa'id: 7/159, with some variation in the hadith.]]

Ibrahim ibn Abi Yahya, from Abu al-Hurayn, from Abu 'Abd Allah al-Shami, who said: "Whoever recites the surah of al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran on the night of Friday, he will be given on the Day of Resurrection two wings with which he will fly over the Sirat." [4] [[Mizan al-I'tidal: 2/424, where it says: two wings strung with pearls and rubies.]]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Zubayr, and Muhammad ibn Marwan from al-Kalbi, and 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far al-Razi from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: This was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran. They were sixty riders who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and among them were fourteen men of their nobles. Among the fourteen were three men to whom their affairs returned: al-'Aqib, who was their commander and the one who advised them, and whose opinion they never departed from, and his name was 'Abd al-Masih; and al-Sayyid [their scholar] and the owner of their caravan, whose name was [al-Ayham, also said: Shurahbil]; and Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah, who was considered their rabbi (scholar), their leader, and the head of their schools. He had been honored among them and had taught their priests because of the goodness of his work in their religion, and the kings of Rome had honored him [and enriched him and built for him] churches, because of his knowledge and diligence.

So they came to the Messenger of Allah in Madinah and entered his mosque, after he had prayed the 'Asr, wearing striped Yemeni garments and cloaks fastened with clasps, in the finery of men of Bali al-Harith [for ease of pronunciation; originally: Banu al-Harith] ibn Ka'b. Some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) who saw them said: "We have never seen a delegation like them!" Their prayer time came, so they stood and prayed in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they prayed facing the east.

The sayyid and the 'aqib spoke with the Messenger of Allah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Submit (aslimu)." They said: "We submitted before you." He said: "You lie. What prevents you from Islam is your claim [in the manuscript: your supplication] that Allah has a son, your worship of the cross, and your eating of pork." They said: "If Allah has no son, then whose son is He?" And they disputed with him all together concerning 'Isa (peace be upon him). The Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: [There is no child except that it resembles its father. They said: Yes. He said: Do you not] know that our Lord is living and does not die, while 'Isa will come to extinction? They said: Yes. He said: Do you not know that our Lord is the Sustainer of everything, who protects it and provides for it? They said: Yes. He said: Does 'Isa possess any of that? They said: No. He said: Do you not know that nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah? They said: Yes. He said: Does 'Isa know any of that except what he was taught? They said: No. He said: Indeed our Lord fashioned 'Isa in the womb as He willed, and our Lord does not eat, drink, or excrete? They said: Yes. He said: Do you not know that 'Isa's mother carried him as a woman carries, then bore him as a woman bears her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, and he ate, drank, and excreted? They said: Yes. He said: Then how can this be as you claim? So they fell silent.

Then Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them the beginning of the surah of Al 'Imran, up to some eighty verses of it.

He, the Mighty, the Majestic, said: Alif Lam Mim.

Ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr and al-Qa'qa' al-Madani recited ' Alif Lam Mim' separated, and likewise all the disjointed letters with which surahs begin.

Ibn Ja'far al-Rawwasi, al-A'mash and al-Harami recited "Alif Lam Mim. Allah" with a cut (qat'), while the rest read it connected (wasl), with the mim fathah. As for the one who pronounces the mim with fathah and connects, there are two explanations:

The Basrans said: Because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (sakinayn), the vowel was moved to the lightest vowel.

The Kufans said: It was originally unvocalized, because the letters of the alphabet are built on pausal form (waqf). When the hamzat al-wasl came upon it, the alif was elided and the letter was pronounced continuously, so its vowel, the fathah, was transferred to the mim.

As for the one who cuts (qat'), he has two explanations:

The first: intending a pause, then cutting the hamzah for beginning, like the words of the poet:
"You will surely hear soon in their abodes: Allah is greatest, O vengeance for 'Uthman!"
[[al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah: 7/219; Taj al-'Arus: 3/70.]]

The second: that he treats it according to the dialect of those who pronounce the hamzat al-wasl as a full hamzah.
Like the words of the poet:
"When one exceeds two, it is revealed; and it is a daughter, and the multiplying of slanderers is worthy of it." [[al-Sihah: 1/294.]]

As for the one who separates and cuts, it is for magnification and exaltation: "Allah" is a beginning, and what follows is its predicate. "There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer" is its description. "He has sent down upon you the Book": Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla recited "nazala" with a light zay, and "al-kitab" with a raised ba'; the rest read it with a shadda on the zay and a fathah on the ba', for multiplicity, because the Qur'an was revealed in stages, piece by piece, and tanzil occurs repeatedly. He said: "And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel," because those two were revealed all at once. "He has sent down upon you, O Muhammad, the Book," the Qur'an, "with truth," with justice and sincerity. "Confirming": agreeing with "what lies between its hands," that is, what came before it of the scriptures, in matters of monotheism, prophethood, reports, and some legislation.

"And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel." The Basrans said: its origin is "wawriyah," from dawalah and harqalah. The first waw was changed into a ta', and the open ya' was made an alif, so it became "tawrah," then it was written with a ya' according to the root of the word. The Kufans said: it is "taf'alah," and the reason for it is what we have mentioned, like "tawsiyah" and "tawfiyah," so the ya' was changed into an alif, as the Tayy tribe does, saying to a girl "jaraah," and to a forelock "nasah." Its root comes from the saying "warra al-zand" when its fire is brought out, and I have transformed it. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: "Have you seen the fire that you kindle?" [[Surah al-Waqi'ah: 71.]] and He said: "By the sparking horses, striking sparks" [[Surah al-'Adiyat: 2.]]. It is called "tawrah" because it is light and radiance, indicated by His saying: "And a radiance and a reminder for the God-fearing" [[Surah al-Anbiya': 48.]]. This was said by al-Farra' and most scholars. [Al-Mu'arrij] said: it is from "tawriyah," which is concealing a thing and alluding to something else.

From the hadith: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "when he intended something, he concealed it by means of something else" [5].

Most tawriyah is by allusion and hinting, without clarity and explicit statement. It was also said: in Hebrew it is "nurwatho," meaning: the Law.

"Injil" is better than "najl," which is emergence, and from it a child is called "najl" because of its coming out.

Al-A'sha said:
"He was a noble son in the times his parents bore him, since they bore him, and what a good thing they bore."
[[al-Sihah: 1/222.]]

It was named thus because Allah the Exalted brought out through it what had been effaced of the truth, restoring it. It is also said that it is from "al-mutanajjal," which is breadth of the earth; one says: "I cut it wide (najlan)," meaning broad. It was named thus because it is a source which He brought out for them and widened for them as light and radiance. It was also said: in Syriac it is "anqlyun," meaning: the Law.

Al-Hasan read "al-Anjil" with a fathah on the hamzah; the rest read it with a kasrah, like "al-Iklil."

"From before" is raised as a termination (ghayah), and the termination here is the cutting off of the Book from it, like His saying: "To Allah belongs the command, from before and from after" [Surah al-Rum: 4]. And Zuhayr said:
"Whatever good they performed, it was only inherited by the fathers of their fathers before."
[[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 3/173.]]

"A guidance for the people": a guide for whoever follows it, and it did not end, because it is a verbal noun, and it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state and a cut-off.

"And He sent down the Criterion (al-Furqan)": the distinction between truth and falsehood. Al-Suddi said: there is inversion and displacement in the verse; its meaning is: "And He sent down the Torah, the Gospel, and the Criterion as guidance for the God-fearing."

"Indeed those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah, for them is a severe punishment, and Allah is Mighty, Owner of retribution."

"Indeed nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden from Allah. He is the One who fashions you in the wombs as He wills: male and female, short and tall, black and white, handsome and ugly, happy and wretched."

"There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise."

"He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), perfected, clear, and detailed."

"They are the Mother of the Book," meaning: its origin, upon which rulings are based; it gathers the lawful and the unlawful, and it is set aside for the people of Islam. And they are the verses of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an, and in every book that the people of every religion accept, and about which the people of every land do not differ.

The Arabs call everything excellent and comprehensive, which serves as a reference for a people, by such names: as the Preserved Tablet is called "Mother of the Book," al-Fatihah "Mother of the Qur'an," Makkah "Mother of the Towns," the brain "Mother of the Head," the mother "umm," the banner "umm," the man who manages the affairs of the household "umm," and the cow, camel, or sheep by which the people of a house live "umm." 'Isa (peace be upon him) used to say to water: "This is my father," and to bread: "This is my mother," because the sustenance of bodies depends on them.

He said "Mother of the Book" and did not say "mothers of the books," because all the verses, in their completeness and unity, are like a single verse, and the speech of Allah is one.

It was also said: its meaning is a single word; so "they are the Mother of the Book," as He said: "And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign" [Surah al-Mu'minun: 50], meaning each of them is a sign.

"And others (akhar)": the plural of "ukhra." It is not declined because it is a derivative of "awakhir," like "Umar" and "Zufar." This is what al-Kisa'i said.

It was also said: its "akhar" was left undeclined because it is an adjective, like "jam'" and "kas'," which are not declined because they are adjectives.

It was also said: because it is built on "wahidah" in not taking tanwin, and another "wahidah" is undeclined.

"Mutashabihat": they resemble one another. The scholars differed concerning the muhkam and the mutashabih. Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, and al-Suddi said: "The muhkam is the abrogating (nasikh) by which one acts." "The mutashabih is the abrogated (mansukh) which is believed in but not acted upon; this is a report from 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas."

'Ali ibn Abi Talhah narrated from him, saying: "The muhkamat of the Qur'an are the abrogating, its lawful and unlawful, its limits, its obligations, and what is commanded and acted upon."

And the mutashabihat: its abrogated, its preceding and succeeding, its parables, its oaths, and what is believed in but not acted upon.

Zuhayr ibn Mu'awiyah, from Abu Ishaq, said: Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His saying, "Among them are verses that are muhkamat": they are the three verses in Surah al-An'am, "Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you..." [Surah al-An'am: 151] up to the end of the three verses; its counterpart in Surah al-Isra' is "Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him..." [Surah al-Isra': 23] and the verses.

Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: "The muhkam is what contains the lawful and the unlawful, and whatever is other than that is mutashabih, [confirming] one another."

Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The muhkam is that which does not admit of more than one interpretation. The mutashabih is that which admits of several interpretations.

Ibn al-Zubayr said: Among the muhkam is what Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book of the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them), explained and made clear for Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, such as the story of Nuh, mentioned in twenty-four verses; the story of Hud in ten verses; the story of Salih in eight verses; the story of Ibrahim in eight verses; the story of Lut in eight verses; the story of Shu'ayb in ten verses; and the story of Musa in many verses.

And [the verses of] the hadith of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are mentioned in twenty-four verses.

The mutashabih is what the wording differs in their stories when repeated, as He said in one place concerning the story of Nuh: "We said: Carry in it..." [Surah Hud: 40], and in another place: "So load in it..." [Surah al-Mu'minun: 27].

And concerning the staff of Musa He said: "Then behold, it was a snake moving swiftly" [Surah Ta-Ha: 20], and in another place He said: "a manifest serpent" [Surah al-A'raf: 107], and similar.

Some of them said: "The muhkam is what the scholars know its interpretation and understand its meaning."

"The mutashabih is what no one has a way to know, of what Allah has kept to Himself knowledge of," such as the report of the time of the emergence of the Dajjal, the descent of 'Isa, the rising of the sun from the west, the establishment of the Hour, and the passing away and ending of the world.

Abu Fakhitah said: "The muhkamat, which are the Mother of the Book, are the openings of the surahs, from which the Qur'an is extracted. Alif Lam Mim. 'That is the Book, there is no doubt in it' [Surah al-Baqarah: 1-2]: from it al-Baqarah was extracted; and 'Alif Lam Mim. Allah' [Surah Al 'Imran: 1-2]: from it Al 'Imran was extracted."

Ibn Kaysan said: "The muhkamat have clear proofs and manifest indications; whoever hears them has no need to seek their meanings in the mutashabih, whose knowledge is doubtful; by reflecting on it, the common people recognize the detail of the truth in it from falsehood."

Some of them said: "The muhkam is what there is consensus upon its interpretation, and the mutashabih is what its meaning is not clear."

Abu 'Uthman said: The muhkam is the Opening of the Book (Fatihat al-Kitab).

Al-Sha'bi said: I saw in some tafsirs [see Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/242, from the tafsir of al-Mawardi, and Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/10] that the mutashabih is [what its wording is obscure, while the muhkam is what its wording is clear; and on this basis the whole Qur'an is] muhkam from one aspect in meaning [with strength] [.....] [an illegible word], as Allah said: "A Book whose verses have been made precise" [Surah Hud: 1].

And the mutashabih from one aspect is that it resembles one part of it another in beauty and confirms one another.

Ibn 'Abbas, in the narration of Shadhan, said: The mutashabih is the disjointed letters at the beginnings of surahs. That is because the rulers of the Jews, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and their like, came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and Huyayy said to him: "It has reached us that 'Alif Lam Mim' was revealed to you. Was it revealed to you?" He said: "Yes." Huyayy said: "If that is true, I know the lifespan of your community, which is seventy-one years. Has anything else been revealed to you?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Ra'" [Surah Yunus: 1]. Huyayy said: "This is greater than that; it is seventy-one and a hundred years. Has anything else been revealed?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Mim Sad" [Surah al-A'raf: 1]. He said: "This is greater than that; it is one hundred and sixty-one years. Has more been revealed?" He said: "Yes, Alif Lam Ra'" [Surah Hud? / Yunus]. He said: "This is more than a hundred and seventy years. You have confused us, and we do not know whether to take from its abundance or its little. We are among those who do not believe in this."

Then Allah the Exalted revealed: "He it is who sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are muhkamat, they are the Mother of the Book, and others that are mutashabihat. As for those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)": that is, a turning away from the truth. It was also said: doubt.

"They follow that which is mutashabih of it": the scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse.

Al-Rabi' said: They are the delegation of Najran, who disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not know that he is the Word of Allah and a Spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us," so Allah revealed this verse.

Al-Kalbi said: They are the Jews. [Ajhal] this Ummah in extracting it by the reckoning of the abjad. Ibn Jurayj said: They are the hypocrites.

[Al-Qa'ila] al-Hasan said: They are the Khawarij.

Qatadah, when he recited this verse, "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," said: "If they are not others, then they are the Sabaiyya, and I do not know who they are."

Some of them said: They are all the innovators (muhdathah).

Hammad ibn Salamah, Abu al-Walid Yazid ibn Abi Maytham and his father all narrated together from 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book," and then he (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who ask about what is mutashabih of it and dispute concerning it, they are those whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has meant; so beware of them and do not associate with them." [6] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/9, with variation; Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 2/5, from several chains that vary.]]

"Seeking discord (ibtigha' al-fitnah)": seeking shirk, said al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn al-Zubayr, and Mujahid: seeking doubts and confusion, so that they may lead their ignorant astray by them.

**Ta'wil** (the interpretation or ultimate meaning) of it: its explanation and knowledge. The evidence is His saying, ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾ [18:78].

It was also said: the seeking of its outcome, and the seeking of the term of the lifespan of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community, from the reckoning of the abjad (numerical value of letters). The evidence is His saying, ﴿That is better and more excellent in outcome (ta'wil)﴾ [4:59], meaning its outcome. Its origin is from the saying of the Arabs, "taawwala al-fata" (the young man reached his end), when he has reached maturity.

Al-A'sha said:

*"Because she was, [in her affection], taking the outcome of her love,*
*as the spring-born foal's mother took its outcome and it grew up."*
