This is shown by His saying ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and more﴾ [Yunus 10:26], and His saying ﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation covers them﴾ [Yunus 10:27], and His saying ﴿Faces that day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:22], and ﴿faces that day will be overcast﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:24].

Then He explained their state and their end, saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ There is an ellipsis here, meaning: it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve after your faith?" Scholars differed about it. al-Rabi' narrated from Abu al-'Aliya from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that they are everyone who disbelieved after his faith in Allah on the Day of the Covenant, when He brought them out from the loins of Adam (peace be upon him) and said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172]. Allah the Mighty and Majestic will recognise them on the Day of Resurrection by their disbelief, and say: "Did you disbelieve after your faith on the Day of the Covenant?"

al-Hasan said: they are the hypocrites who gave the word of faith with their tongues, but denied it in their hearts and deeds.

Yunus ibn Abi Muslim said: I asked 'Ikrima about this verse, and he said: "If I were to explain it, I would not finish its explanation in three days; but I will summarise it for you. These are a people of the People of the Book who believed in their prophets and affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent; when he was sent, they disbelieved in him. That is His saying: 'Did you disbelieve after your faith?'"

Others said: they are from our religious community.

al-Harith al-A'war said: I heard 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) on the pulpit saying: "A man leaves his family and does not return to them until he has done a deed that merits Paradise; and a man leaves his family and does not return to them until he has done a deed that merits the Fire." Then he recited ﴿On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black...﴾ the verse.

Then "He called out to those who disbelieved after faith [Did you disbelieve?]" — evidence for this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There will come upon my community a time when a man wakes up a believer and in the evening is a disbeliever, selling his religion for a small share of the world's goods."

Abu Umama al-Bahili said: they are the Kharijites (al-Khawarij). Qatada said: they are all the people of innovations.

The evidence for these interpretations is His saying ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar 39:60], and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There will surely be people from my companions who will be driven away from the Pool, until when I see them they will be pulled away from me, and I will say: 'My companions, my companions!' It will be said to me: 'You do not know what they innovated after you; they turned back on their heels.'"

﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾: these are the people of His obedience and the fulfilment of His covenant. ﴿Then in Allah's mercy﴾: the Garden of Allah. ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾, up to ﴿and Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, that is, He does not punish them without guilt.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned. You are the best community ever brought forth...﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:109–110]. Ikrima and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh, and Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, because Ibn al-Sayf and Wahb ibn Yahud, the two Jews, said to them: "Our religion is better than what you call us to, and we are better and more excellent than you." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ refers to those who emigrated with the Prophet (ﷺ) to Medina. Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak: they are the Companions of Muhammad specifically, the transmitters and callers whom Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded to obey. This is supported by what al-Suddi narrated, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said concerning ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "It applies to our first ones and does not apply to our later ones."

'Umar ibn al-Husayn narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Blessed is whoever sees me, and whoever sees one who saw me, and whoever sees one who saw one who saw one who saw one who saw me." [The manuscript repeats this phrase.]

al-A'mash narrated from Abu Salih from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile my Companions, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, he would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it."

Others said: they are the whole body of believers of this community. His saying ﴿you were﴾ means "you are," like His saying ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?﴾ [Maryam 19:29], meaning "who is in the cradle." Inserting "kana" (was) and omitting it in such a sense has the same meaning, as in His saying ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-A'raf 7:86], and in another place ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-Anfal 8:26].

Muhammad ibn Jarir [al-Tabari] said: this is in the sense of completeness, and its interpretation is: "you were created and found to be the best community."

He also said: the meaning of ﴿you were the best community﴾ is with Allah in the Preserved Tablet. ﴿Brought forth for mankind﴾: some said: "for mankind" is connected to His saying "the best community," meaning: you are the best of mankind for mankind. Abu Hurayra said: its meaning is "you were the best of people for people, bringing them in chains and admitting them into Islam." Qatada said: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), to whom no prophet before him was commanded to fight; so they take captives from among the Romans, Turks, and non-Arabs and bring them into their religion. So they are "the best community brought forth for mankind."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: no other community among the followers of religions enjoins good and forbids evil towards the others and themselves, so that none of them wrongs another; rather they enjoin them to do right and forbid them from wrong. Therefore the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the nations of mankind.

Others said: "for mankind" is connected to His saying "brought forth," and its meaning is: Allah has not brought forth for mankind a community better than the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); so they are the best community that has been established and brought forth for mankind. Reports have followed this interpretation.

Bahz ibn Hakim narrated from his father, from his grandfather, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say concerning His saying ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "You will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured by Allah the Mighty and Majestic."

'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah narrated from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise are a hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them from this community."

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no nation but that some of it is in the Fire and some in Paradise, but all of my community is in Paradise."

Thabit al-Bunani narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of my community is like rain: one does not know whether its beginning is better or its end."

It is narrated from Anas, who said: A bishop (usquf) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that he had seen in his dream the nations being prevented on the Bridge [.......] [an illegible word], until the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) came, radiant and with white marks. He said: "I said: 'Who are these, prophets?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Messengers?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Angels?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Who are these?'"

They said: "The community of Muhammad (ﷺ), radiant with white marks, upon them the traces of ablution." When the bishop awoke, he embraced Islam.

It is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from 'Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Paradise was forbidden to all the prophets until I enter it, and it was forbidden to the nations until my community enters it."

Abu Burda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My community is a merciful community. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will give every man of this community a man from among the disbelievers and say: 'This is your ransom from the Fire.'"

It is narrated from Anas, who said: I went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and suddenly a voice came from a ravine. He said: "O Anas, go and see what this voice is." I went and found a man praying towards a tree, saying: "O Allah, make me one of the merciful community of Muhammad, forgiven, whose supplications are answered, and whose repentance is accepted." I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "Go and tell him: the Messenger of Allah sends you greetings and says: 'Who are you?'" I went to him and informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said. He said: "Convey my greetings to the Messenger of Allah and say: 'Your brother al-Khidr says: I ask [You] (أسألك) that You make me of your merciful community, forgiven, whose supplications are answered, and whose repentance is accepted.'" [A blank in the photographed manuscript; the apparent reading is what we have given.]

It was said to 'Isa (peace be upon him): "O Spirit of Allah, is there a community after this community?" He said: "Scholars, forbearing, wise, righteous, pious, as if they were prophets in knowledge; they are content with little provision from Allah, and Allah is content with little deed from them; He will admit them into Paradise by the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

We have been told that Ka'b al-Ahbar was asked: "Why did you not embrace Islam in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, but embraced it in the time of 'Umar?" He said: "Because my father gave me a sealed book and said: 'Do not break its seal.' Then during the days of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), I saw in a dream someone who said to me: 'Your father betrayed you concerning that document.' So I broke it, and in it was the description of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ): Salwoma, 'Alwoma, Hakuma, Safuha, and Kharuja." They asked him about its interpretation, and he said: "It means that their sign is that some of them greet others with peace; their scholars are like the prophets of the Children of Israel; Allah's judgment for them is Paradise; they shake hands, and they are forgiven and emerge from their sins as on the day their mothers bore them."

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: This verse is a praise of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and He would not praise a people and then punish them.

Then He mentioned their virtues, saying: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ up to ﴿they will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, the verse. Muqatil said: The chiefs of the Jews, Ka'b, 'Adi, al-Nu'man, Abu Rafi', Abu Yasir, Kinana and Abu Suriya, targeted their believers, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, harming them for their Islam. So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿They will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, meaning: they will not harm you, O believers, these Jews, except with hurt by the tongue, that is, threats and slander. It was also said: [it means] a call to misguidance. And it was said: a word of disbelief, which if they hear it from them, they will be hurt by it. ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ in flight, and this is a jussive (jazm) as the answer to the conditional, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾. He began a new clause [[i.e., made thumma (then) a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) particle, not a conjunctive one; had he made it conjunctive, the verb after it would be in the jussive.]] for the sake of the ends of verses, since they end in the nūn, like His saying ﴿and they will not be given leave, so they will not make excuses﴾ [[Al-Mursalat: 36.]]. Its implied sense is: then they will not be helped.

He said in another place: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [[Fatir: 36.]], since it was not the end of a verse.

The poet said:
"Have you not asked the old abode, so that it would speak?"
That is, so that it would speak [i.e., the fa' introduces the subjunctive, as it is governed by the verb].

Al-Akhfash said: His saying ﴿they will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna') disconnected from the beginning of the speech, like the Arabs' saying: "He complains of nothing except good," and God, exalted is He, said ﴿They will not taste therein coolness or drink, except boiling water and dark pus﴾ [[Al-Naba': 24–25.]], and because this hurt does not harm them. Its meaning is: "but [they do cause] hurt."

﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾: wherever they are found and encountered, meaning: wherever they are met they are overcome, made weak, and killed, so they will not believe, ﴿except with a rope﴾: a covenant from God, ﴿and a rope from the people﴾: Muhammad and the believers, who return the tribute to them, and so they grant them security. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "unless they hold fast to a rope," like the poet's saying:
"She saw me with her ropes and turned away, out of fear,
and in the rope there is a frightened heart that trembles."
That is, she approached with her ropes.

Another said:
"The recurring days have bent me until
I seem like a crouching hunter approaching prey,
Near of step; whoever sees me thinks
I am not shackled, though I am in shackles."
That is: "whoever sees me" [is] "shackled [with a shackle]" [[In the manuscript: "for a shackle".]].

﴿They have incurred wrath from God﴾ up to ﴿They are not all alike﴾, the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: When 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tha'laba ibn Sa'id, Usayd ibn Sa'id, Asad ibn 'Ubayd, and others of the Jews embraced Islam, the chiefs of the Jews said: "None believed in Muhammad except our wicked ones; if they had been among our best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers," and they said to them: "You have lost, since you have exchanged your religion for another." [[Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas: 2/45.]] So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿They are not all alike﴾. "Alike" (sawa') requires two or more things. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse. Some said: the speech contains an implied element, its meaning being: ﴿They are not alike [[As in the manuscript; there is a sign of omission over the word sawa', but no note on this omission is recorded in the margin of the manuscript's photograph.]] from among the People of the Book: a community standing [upright], and another that is not standing,﴾ so the other is omitted, because he mentioned one of the two groups, like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:
"I disobeyed the heart in regard to her command,
though I am obedient to it; I do not know whether the guidance of her seekers
[is in her command] or error."
He meant: "whether it is guidance or error," and omitted it because the speech indicates it.

This is a collective, preceding statement, like their saying: "The mosquitoes bit me" and "Your companions went away." Others said: The complete statement ends at His saying ﴿They are not alike﴾, and this is a pause, because the mention of the two groups of the People of the Book has already occurred in His saying ﴿Among them are believers, and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Then He said ﴿They are not alike﴾, meaning the believers and the defiantly disobedient. Then He described the defiantly disobedient, saying ﴿They will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, then He described the believers, saying ﴿a community standing﴾, the verse. So it refers back to the beginning of the speech, and this is the preference of Muhammad ibn Jarir [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/71.]] and al-Zajjaj. He said: "If you wish, you may make His saying ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾ the beginning of another statement, since the mention of the two groups has already occurred, then He said: 'These two groups are not alike,' and then began, saying: ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾."

Ibn Mas'ud said: its meaning is that the Jews and the community of Muhammad are not equal; the "standing" community is one that upholds the command of God, exalted is He, meaning one that is steadfast upon the upright truth. Ibn 'Abbas said: "a community standing" means guided, standing upon the command of God, not abandoning it as the others abandoned and neglected it. Mujahid: just. Al-Suddi: obedient, standing upon the Book of God, His obligations, and His limits. It was also said: standing in prayer. Al-Akhfash said: "a community standing" means possessing a standing community, and the "ummah" is a way, from their saying "amamtu al-shay'," meaning I aimed at it. Al-Nabigha said:
"Does one who possesses a path, while obedient, take counsel?"
That is, one who possesses a way.
The meaning of the verse is: two who have an upright way.

﴿They recite the signs of God﴾: they read the Book of God. Mujahid said: they follow, as it is said: "talahu," meaning he followed him. The poet said:
"You have made my bucket pour me down,
and I do not desire the follower of the companion..."
[Al-Sihah: 6/2273.]
"Indeed I did not desire them [...]" [[Two words not legible.]]
That is, you make me follow you.

﴿In the hours of the night﴾, that is, its hours, and its singular is "ini," like "nahi" and "anhaa'," and "ina" like "ma'a."
The poet said:
"Sweet and bitter, like the bending of an arrow is its disposition,
in every ini of the night's hours it puts on its shoes..." [[Lisan al-'Arab: 14/50, "ina".]]
That is, it entertains him in the hours of the night with a matter that passed and did not delay.
The rajiz in the other dialect said:
"By God, how excellent is Ja'far, what a youth,
girding up his leg in every ini."
Al-Suddi said: "hours of the night" means its middle.

Al-Awza'i related from Hassan 'Atiyya, who said: We were told that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two rak'ahs that a servant performs in the middle of the night are better for him than the world and what is in it, and had it not been difficult for my community, I would have made them obligatory upon them." [106] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/368.]]

﴿And they prostrate﴾, that is, they pray, because recitation does not occur in bowing or prostration. Its parallel is His saying:
"And to Him they prostrate," that is, they pray. In the Qur'an: ﴿And when it is said to them, prostrate to the Most Merciful﴾ [[Al-Furqan: 60.]], that is, pray; and His saying ﴿So prostrate to God and worship﴾ [[Al-Najm: 62.]].

They differed concerning the revelation and meaning of the verse. Some said: it concerns the night prayer. From Majma' ibn Yahya al-Ansari, from a man of the Banu Shayba who used to study the books, who said: "We find a speech from the speech of [the Lord] [[In the manuscript: "the Arabs".]]: 'Does the herdsman of camels and sheep think, when night covers him and he is withdrawn, that he is standing and prostrating in the hours of the night?'"

Ibn Mas'ud said: it concerns the 'Atama prayer; they pray it while the People of the Book around them do not pray it.

'Asim, from Zirr, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) delayed the 'Isha' prayer, then went out to the mosque and found the people waiting for the prayer. He said: "Indeed there is no one among the religions who remembers God, mighty and majestic, at this hour except you." [107] [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/396; Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 79.]]
Then God revealed this verse: ﴿They are not alike﴾ up to His saying ﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾

Al-Thawri related from Mansur, who said: We were told that it was revealed concerning people who used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

'Ata said concerning His saying ﴿They are not alike. Among the People of the Book is a community standing﴾, the verse: it refers to forty men from the people of Najran of the Arabs, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Rum, who were upon the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Among the Ansar were a number of them before the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ), including As'ad ibn Zurara, al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, Muhammad ibn Maslama, and Abu Qays Harma [[As in the manuscript.]] ibn Anas. They were monotheists, performing ritual washing from major impurity, and acknowledging what they knew of the laws of the Hanifiyya, until God, mighty and majestic, brought them the Prophet (ﷺ), so they affirmed him and supported him.

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾. Al-A'mash, Hamza, Yahya, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read with the yā' in both places, as news about the upright community. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu 'Ubayda. The others read with the tā' in both places, in the address form, like His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim. Abu 'Amr regarded both readings, the yā' and the tā', as valid.

The meaning of the verse, ﴿whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾: they will not be deprived of its reward, and their reward will not be denied; rather, it will be thanked [for them] [[In the manuscript: "for you".]] and they will be recompensed for it. ﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing﴾: the believers.

And let there be among you a community (umma) [meaning: and let you be a community], as in His saying ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj 22:30]. He did not intend "shun the abomination of idols"; rather, the original is "shun the idols, for they are an abomination" (وإنها رجس). The lam in His saying وَلْتَكُنْ is the lam of command (لام الأمر, lam al-amr). ﴿Who invite to good﴾: Islam. ﴿And enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾, and ﴿those are the successful﴾.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "We heard Ibn al-Zubayr recite: (Let there be among you a community who enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and seek help against what afflicts them)." A similar reading is narrated from 'Uthman [........] [a blank in the photographed manuscript].

**Chapter on enjoining good and forbidding evil**

Hassan ibn Sulayman narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the successor (khalifa) of Allah on His earth, the successor of His Messenger, and the successor of His Book."

It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, from Durra bint Abi Lahab, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on the pulpit and said: "O Messenger of Allah, who is the best of people?" He said: "The one who most enjoins what is right, most forbids what is wrong, is most mindful of Allah the Exalted, and is most dutiful to his kin."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, we do not act [upon what is right] to the extent that nothing of the good remains that we have not enjoined ourselves to, and we refrain from the wrong to the extent that nothing of the wrong remains that we have not refrained from; and we neither enjoin the good nor forbid the wrong [i.e., we are concerned only with ourselves]." He said: "Enjoin what is right even if you do not practise it, and forbid what is wrong even if you do not abstain from all of it."

Al-Sha'bi narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the sinner among a people is like a people who boarded a ship and divided it among themselves, so each person got a share of it. One of them took an axe and began to chisel at his own place. His companions said to him: 'What are you doing? Do you want to sink it and sink us too?' He said: 'It is my place.' If they seize his hand, they all are saved, and he is saved; but if they leave him, he sinks and they sink."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, said: "The best jihad is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and hatred of the wicked. Whoever enjoins what is right strengthens the back of the believer; whoever forbids what is wrong humbles the nose of the hypocrite; and whoever hates the hypocrites and becomes angry for the sake of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, Allah the Exalted becomes angry on his behalf."

Abu al-Darda' said: "You must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or Allah will set over you a tyrannical ruler who will not honour your elder nor show mercy to your young; your best will supplicate but not be answered, they will seek victory but not be given it, and they will seek forgiveness but not be forgiven."

Hudhayfa al-Yamani said: "A time will come upon people when the carcass of a donkey among them will be dearer to them than a believer who enjoins them to do right and forbids them from wrong."

Al-Thawri said: "If a man is loved by his neighbours and praised by the people, know that he is a flatterer (mudahin)."

﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾, the verse [Al 'Imran 3:105]. Most exegetes (mufassirun) said: they are the Jews and Christians. Others said: they are the innovators (mubtadi'a) of this community.

'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad narrated: Abu Umama and I stood at the heads of the Harurites (al-Haruriyya, the early Kharijite group) in Syria, at the gate of Homs or Damascus. He said to them: "Dogs of the Fire, dogs of the Fire," twice or three times. "The worst of the slain, and the best of the slain are those they killed." [It was] said: "Is this from an opinion you hold, or something you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "If it were from an opinion I held, I would be very bold. I have not heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except once or twice—until he counted seven times—and I have not narrated it." A man said: "I saw your eyes filled with tears." He said: "It is a mercy that I had for them, for they were believers and then disbelieved after their faith." Then he recited ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾ up to ﴿after your faith﴾, and then said: "They are the Harurites."

Qabisa narrated from Jabir that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), when he arrived at a gate of Damascus called al-Jabiya, praised Allah and extolled Him as He deserves, then said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us as I stand among you, and said: 'Whoever desires the centre of Paradise should cling to the community, for Satan is with the lone one (al-fadh, the single individual), and from two he is further away.'"

﴿On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black, ...﴾: "a day" (يوم) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, meaning "on a day"; and the accusative of the time-expression here is by analogy with the object (التشبيه بالمفعول). Yahya ibn Wathhab read (تِبيض وتِسود) with a kasra on both taʼs, in the dialect of Tamim.

al-Zuhri read (تبياض وتسواد). As for those whose faces turned black...

The meaning: the faces of the believers become white and the faces of the disbelievers become black. It is also said: on the day when the faces of the sincere become white and the faces of the hypocrites become black.

'Ata said: the faces of the Emigrants and the Helpers become white, and the faces of Qurayza and al-Nadir become black.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black": he said: the faces of the People of the Sunna become white, and the faces of the People of Innovation become black.

al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: On the Day of Resurrection, for each people is raised what they used to worship, and each people go to what they used to worship, which is His saying ﴿We shall leave him to what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:115]. When they reach it, they grieve, and their faces turn black from grief. The People of the Qibla (Muslims), the Jews and the Christians remain, not knowing anything of what has been raised for them. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic comes to them, and those who used to prostrate in worldly life, obedient and believing, prostrate to Him. The People of the Book and the hypocrites remain as if they cannot prostrate. Then they are permitted, and they raise their heads, and the faces of the believers are whiter than snow; and the hypocrites and the People of the Book stand as if there were spikes (al-safafid) in their backs. When they look at the faces of the believers and their whiteness, they grieve a severe grief and their faces turn black, and they say: "Our Lord, You have blackened the faces of those who worship other than You; so why are our faces blackened? By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists!" Allah says to the angels: "Look how they lied against themselves."

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the whitening of faces is their brightness, joy, and delight in their deeds and Allah's reward; and their blackening is their grief, gloom, and dejection over their deeds and Allah's punishment. This is shown by His saying ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and more﴾ [Yunus 10:26], and His saying ﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation covers them﴾ [Yunus 10:27], and His saying ﴿Faces that day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:22], and ﴿faces that day will be overcast﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:24].

Then He explained their state and their end, saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ There is an ellipsis here, meaning: it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve after your faith?" Scholars differed about it. al-Rabi' narrated from Abu al-'Aliya from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that they are everyone who disbelieved after his faith in Allah on the Day of the Covenant, when He brought them out from the loins of Adam (peace be upon him) and said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172]. Allah the Mighty and Majestic will recognise them on the Day of Resurrection by their disbelief, and say: "Did you disbelieve after your faith on the Day of the Covenant?"

al-Hasan said: they are the hypocrites who gave the word of faith with their tongues, but denied it in their hearts and deeds.

Yunus ibn Abi Muslim said: I asked 'Ikrima about this verse, and he said: "If I were to explain it, I would not finish its explanation in three days; but I will summarise it for you. These are a people of the People of the Book who believed in their prophets and affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent; when he was sent, they disbelieved in him. That is His saying: 'Did you disbelieve after your faith?'"

Others said: they are from our religious community.

al-Harith al-A'war said: I heard 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) on the pulpit saying: "A man leaves his family and does not return to them until he has done a deed that merits Paradise; and a man leaves his family and does not return to them until he has done a deed that merits the Fire." Then he recited ﴿On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black...﴾ the verse.

Then "He called out to those who disbelieved after faith [Did you disbelieve?]" — evidence for this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There will come upon my community a time when a man wakes up a believer and in the evening is a disbeliever, selling his religion for a small share of the world's goods."

Abu Umama al-Bahili said: they are the Kharijites (al-Khawarij). Qatada said: they are all the people of innovations.

The evidence for these interpretations is His saying ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar 39:60], and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There will surely be people from my companions who will be driven away from the Pool, until when I see them they will be pulled away from me, and I will say: 'My companions, my companions!' It will be said to me: 'You do not know what they innovated after you; they turned back on their heels.'"

﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾: these are the people of His obedience and the fulfilment of His covenant. ﴿Then in Allah's mercy﴾: the Garden of Allah. ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾, up to ﴿and Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, that is, He does not punish them without guilt.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned. You are the best community ever brought forth...﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:109–110]. Ikrima and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh, and Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, because Ibn al-Sayf and Wahb ibn Yahud, the two Jews, said to them: "Our religion is better than what you call us to, and we are better and more excellent than you." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ refers to those who emigrated with the Prophet (ﷺ) to Medina. Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak: they are the Companions of Muhammad specifically, the transmitters and callers whom Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded to obey. This is supported by what al-Suddi narrated, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said concerning ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "It applies to our first ones and does not apply to our later ones."

'Umar ibn al-Husayn narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Blessed is whoever sees me, and whoever sees one who saw me, and whoever sees one who saw one who saw one who saw one who saw me." [The manuscript repeats this phrase.]

al-A'mash narrated from Abu Salih from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile my Companions, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, he would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it."

Others said: they are the whole body of believers of this community. His saying ﴿you were﴾ means "you are," like His saying ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?﴾ [Maryam 19:29], meaning "who is in the cradle." Inserting "kana" (was) and omitting it in such a sense has the same meaning, as in His saying ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-A'raf 7:86], and in another place ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-Anfal 8:26].

Muhammad ibn Jarir [al-Tabari] said: this is in the sense of completeness, and its interpretation is: "you were created and found to be the best community."

He also said: the meaning of ﴿you were the best community﴾ is with Allah in the Preserved Tablet. ﴿Brought forth for mankind﴾: some said: "for mankind" is connected to His saying "the best community," meaning: you are the best of mankind for mankind. Abu Hurayra said: its meaning is "you were the best of people for people, bringing them in chains and admitting them into Islam." Qatada said: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), to whom no prophet before him was commanded to fight; so they take captives from among the Romans, Turks, and non-Arabs and bring them into their religion. So they are "the best community brought forth for mankind."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: no other community among the followers of religions enjoins good and forbids evil towards the others and themselves, so that none of them wrongs another; rather they enjoin them to do right and forbid them from wrong. Therefore the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the nations of mankind.

Others said: "for mankind" is connected to His saying "brought forth," and its meaning is: Allah has not brought forth for mankind a community better than the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); so they are the best community that has been established and brought forth for mankind. Reports have followed this interpretation.

Bahz ibn Hakim narrated from his father, from his grandfather, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say concerning His saying ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "You will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured by Allah the Mighty and Majestic."

'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah narrated from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise are a hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them from this community."

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no nation but that some of it is in the Fire and some in Paradise, but all of my community is in Paradise."

Thabit al-Bunani narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of my community is like rain: one does not know whether its beginning is better or its end."

It is narrated from Anas, who said: A bishop (usquf) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that he had seen in his dream the nations being prevented on the Bridge [.......] [an illegible word], until the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) came, radiant and with white marks. He said: "I said: 'Who are these, prophets?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Messengers?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Angels?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Who are these?'"

They said: "The community of Muhammad (ﷺ), radiant with white marks, upon them the traces of ablution." When the bishop awoke, he embraced Islam.

It is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from 'Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Paradise was forbidden to all the prophets until I enter it, and it was forbidden to the nations until my community enters it."

Abu Burda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My community is a merciful community. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will give every man of this community a man from among the disbelievers and say: 'This is your ransom from the Fire.'"

It is narrated from Anas, who said: I went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and suddenly a voice came from a ravine. He said: "O Anas, go and see what this voice is." I went and found a man praying towards a tree, saying: "O Allah, make me one of the merciful community of Muhammad, forgiven, whose supplications are answered, and whose repentance is accepted." I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "Go and tell him: the Messenger of Allah sends you greetings and says: 'Who are you?'" I went to him and informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said. He said: "Convey my greetings to the Messenger of Allah and say: 'Your brother al-Khidr says: I ask [You] (أسألك) that You make me of your merciful community, forgiven, whose supplications are answered, and whose repentance is accepted.'" [A blank in the photographed manuscript; the apparent reading is what we have given.]

It was said to 'Isa (peace be upon him): "O Spirit of Allah, is there a community after this community?" He said: "Scholars, forbearing, wise, righteous, pious, as if they were prophets in knowledge; they are content with little provision from Allah, and Allah is content with little deed from them; He will admit them into Paradise by the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

We have been told that Ka'b al-Ahbar was asked: "Why did you not embrace Islam in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, but embraced it in the time of 'Umar?" He said: "Because my father gave me a sealed book and said: 'Do not break its seal.' Then during the days of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), I saw in a dream someone who said to me: 'Your father betrayed you concerning that document.' So I broke it, and in it was the description of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ): Salwoma, 'Alwoma, Hakuma, Safuha, and Kharuja." They asked him about its interpretation, and he said: "It means that their sign is that some of them greet others with peace; their scholars are like the prophets of the Children of Israel; Allah's judgment for them is Paradise; they shake hands, and they are forgiven and emerge from their sins as on the day their mothers bore them."

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: This verse is a praise of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and He would not praise a people and then punish them.

Then He mentioned their virtues, saying: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ up to ﴿they will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, the verse. Muqatil said: The chiefs of the Jews, Ka'b, 'Adi, al-Nu'man, Abu Rafi', Abu Yasir, Kinana and Abu Suriya, targeted their believers, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, harming them for their Islam. So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿They will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, meaning: they will not harm you, O believers, these Jews, except with hurt by the tongue, that is, threats and slander. It was also said: [it means] a call to misguidance. And it was said: a word of disbelief, which if they hear it from them, they will be hurt by it. ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ in flight, and this is a jussive (jazm) as the answer to the conditional, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾. He began a new clause [[i.e., made thumma (then) a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) particle, not a conjunctive one; had he made it conjunctive, the verb after it would be in the jussive.]] for the sake of the ends of verses, since they end in the nūn, like His saying ﴿and they will not be given leave, so they will not make excuses﴾ [[Al-Mursalat: 36.]]. Its implied sense is: then they will not be helped.

He said in another place: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [[Fatir: 36.]], since it was not the end of a verse.

The poet said:
"Have you not asked the old abode, so that it would speak?"
That is, so that it would speak [i.e., the fa' introduces the subjunctive, as it is governed by the verb].

Al-Akhfash said: His saying ﴿they will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna') disconnected from the beginning of the speech, like the Arabs' saying: "He complains of nothing except good," and God, exalted is He, said ﴿They will not taste therein coolness or drink, except boiling water and dark pus﴾ [[Al-Naba': 24–25.]], and because this hurt does not harm them. Its meaning is: "but [they do cause] hurt."

﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾: wherever they are found and encountered, meaning: wherever they are met they are overcome, made weak, and killed, so they will not believe, ﴿except with a rope﴾: a covenant from God, ﴿and a rope from the people﴾: Muhammad and the believers, who return the tribute to them, and so they grant them security. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "unless they hold fast to a rope," like the poet's saying:
"She saw me with her ropes and turned away, out of fear,
and in the rope there is a frightened heart that trembles."
That is, she approached with her ropes.

Another said:
"The recurring days have bent me until
I seem like a crouching hunter approaching prey,
Near of step; whoever sees me thinks
I am not shackled, though I am in shackles."
That is: "whoever sees me" [is] "shackled [with a shackle]" [[In the manuscript: "for a shackle".]].

﴿They have incurred wrath from God﴾ up to ﴿They are not all alike﴾, the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: When 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tha'laba ibn Sa'id, Usayd ibn Sa'id, Asad ibn 'Ubayd, and others of the Jews embraced Islam, the chiefs of the Jews said: "None believed in Muhammad except our wicked ones; if they had been among our best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers," and they said to them: "You have lost, since you have exchanged your religion for another." [[Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas: 2/45.]] So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿They are not all alike﴾. "Alike" (sawa') requires two or more things. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse. Some said: the speech contains an implied element, its meaning being: ﴿They are not alike [[As in the manuscript; there is a sign of omission over the word sawa', but no note on this omission is recorded in the margin of the manuscript's photograph.]] from among the People of the Book: a community standing [upright], and another that is not standing,﴾ so the other is omitted, because he mentioned one of the two groups, like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:
"I disobeyed the heart in regard to her command,
though I am obedient to it; I do not know whether the guidance of her seekers
[is in her command] or error."
He meant: "whether it is guidance or error," and omitted it because the speech indicates it.

This is a collective, preceding statement, like their saying: "The mosquitoes bit me" and "Your companions went away." Others said: The complete statement ends at His saying ﴿They are not alike﴾, and this is a pause, because the mention of the two groups of the People of the Book has already occurred in His saying ﴿Among them are believers, and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Then He said ﴿They are not alike﴾, meaning the believers and the defiantly disobedient. Then He described the defiantly disobedient, saying ﴿They will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, then He described the believers, saying ﴿a community standing﴾, the verse. So it refers back to the beginning of the speech, and this is the preference of Muhammad ibn Jarir [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/71.]] and al-Zajjaj. He said: "If you wish, you may make His saying ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾ the beginning of another statement, since the mention of the two groups has already occurred, then He said: 'These two groups are not alike,' and then began, saying: ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾."

Ibn Mas'ud said: its meaning is that the Jews and the community of Muhammad are not equal; the "standing" community is one that upholds the command of God, exalted is He, meaning one that is steadfast upon the upright truth. Ibn 'Abbas said: "a community standing" means guided, standing upon the command of God, not abandoning it as the others abandoned and neglected it. Mujahid: just. Al-Suddi: obedient, standing upon the Book of God, His obligations, and His limits. It was also said: standing in prayer. Al-Akhfash said: "a community standing" means possessing a standing community, and the "ummah" is a way, from their saying "amamtu al-shay'," meaning I aimed at it. Al-Nabigha said:
"Does one who possesses a path, while obedient, take counsel?"
That is, one who possesses a way.
The meaning of the verse is: two who have an upright way.

﴿They recite the signs of God﴾: they read the Book of God. Mujahid said: they follow, as it is said: "talahu," meaning he followed him. The poet said:
"You have made my bucket pour me down,
and I do not desire the follower of the companion..."
[Al-Sihah: 6/2273.]
"Indeed I did not desire them [...]" [[Two words not legible.]]
That is, you make me follow you.

﴿In the hours of the night﴾, that is, its hours, and its singular is "ini," like "nahi" and "anhaa'," and "ina" like "ma'a."
The poet said:
"Sweet and bitter, like the bending of an arrow is its disposition,
in every ini of the night's hours it puts on its shoes..." [[Lisan al-'Arab: 14/50, "ina".]]
That is, it entertains him in the hours of the night with a matter that passed and did not delay.
The rajiz in the other dialect said:
"By God, how excellent is Ja'far, what a youth,
girding up his leg in every ini."
Al-Suddi said: "hours of the night" means its middle.

Al-Awza'i related from Hassan 'Atiyya, who said: We were told that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two rak'ahs that a servant performs in the middle of the night are better for him than the world and what is in it, and had it not been difficult for my community, I would have made them obligatory upon them." [106] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/368.]]

﴿And they prostrate﴾, that is, they pray, because recitation does not occur in bowing or prostration. Its parallel is His saying:
"And to Him they prostrate," that is, they pray. In the Qur'an: ﴿And when it is said to them, prostrate to the Most Merciful﴾ [[Al-Furqan: 60.]], that is, pray; and His saying ﴿So prostrate to God and worship﴾ [[Al-Najm: 62.]].

They differed concerning the revelation and meaning of the verse. Some said: it concerns the night prayer. From Majma' ibn Yahya al-Ansari, from a man of the Banu Shayba who used to study the books, who said: "We find a speech from the speech of [the Lord] [[In the manuscript: "the Arabs".]]: 'Does the herdsman of camels and sheep think, when night covers him and he is withdrawn, that he is standing and prostrating in the hours of the night?'"

Ibn Mas'ud said: it concerns the 'Atama prayer; they pray it while the People of the Book around them do not pray it.

'Asim, from Zirr, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) delayed the 'Isha' prayer, then went out to the mosque and found the people waiting for the prayer. He said: "Indeed there is no one among the religions who remembers God, mighty and majestic, at this hour except you." [107] [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/396; Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 79.]]
Then God revealed this verse: ﴿They are not alike﴾ up to His saying ﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾

Al-Thawri related from Mansur, who said: We were told that it was revealed concerning people who used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

'Ata said concerning His saying ﴿They are not alike. Among the People of the Book is a community standing﴾, the verse: it refers to forty men from the people of Najran of the Arabs, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Rum, who were upon the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Among the Ansar were a number of them before the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ), including As'ad ibn Zurara, al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, Muhammad ibn Maslama, and Abu Qays Harma [[As in the manuscript.]] ibn Anas. They were monotheists, performing ritual washing from major impurity, and acknowledging what they knew of the laws of the Hanifiyya, until God, mighty and majestic, brought them the Prophet (ﷺ), so they affirmed him and supported him.

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾. Al-A'mash, Hamza, Yahya, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read with the yā' in both places, as news about the upright community. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu 'Ubayda. The others read with the tā' in both places, in the address form, like His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim. Abu 'Amr regarded both readings, the yā' and the tā', as valid.

The meaning of the verse, ﴿whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾: they will not be deprived of its reward, and their reward will not be denied; rather, it will be thanked [for them] [[In the manuscript: "for you".]] and they will be recompensed for it. ﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing﴾: the believers.

And let there be among you a community (umma) [meaning: and let you be a community], as in His saying ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj 22:30]. He did not intend "shun the abomination of idols"; rather, the original is "shun the idols, for they are an abomination" (وإنها رجس). The lam in His saying وَلْتَكُنْ is the lam of command (لام الأمر, lam al-amr). ﴿Who invite to good﴾: Islam. ﴿And enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾, and ﴿those are the successful﴾.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna narrated from 'Amr ibn Dinar, who said: "We heard Ibn al-Zubayr recite: (Let there be among you a community who enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and seek help against what afflicts them)." A similar reading is narrated from 'Uthman [........] [a blank in the photographed manuscript].

**Chapter on enjoining good and forbidding evil**

Hassan ibn Sulayman narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever enjoins what is right and forbids what is wrong is the successor (khalifa) of Allah on His earth, the successor of His Messenger, and the successor of His Book."

It is narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, from Durra bint Abi Lahab, who said: A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was on the pulpit and said: "O Messenger of Allah, who is the best of people?" He said: "The one who most enjoins what is right, most forbids what is wrong, is most mindful of Allah the Exalted, and is most dutiful to his kin."

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: We said: "O Messenger of Allah, we do not act [upon what is right] to the extent that nothing of the good remains that we have not enjoined ourselves to, and we refrain from the wrong to the extent that nothing of the wrong remains that we have not refrained from; and we neither enjoin the good nor forbid the wrong [i.e., we are concerned only with ourselves]." He said: "Enjoin what is right even if you do not practise it, and forbid what is wrong even if you do not abstain from all of it."

Al-Sha'bi narrated from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of the sinner among a people is like a people who boarded a ship and divided it among themselves, so each person got a share of it. One of them took an axe and began to chisel at his own place. His companions said to him: 'What are you doing? Do you want to sink it and sink us too?' He said: 'It is my place.' If they seize his hand, they all are saved, and he is saved; but if they leave him, he sinks and they sink."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, said: "The best jihad is enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and hatred of the wicked. Whoever enjoins what is right strengthens the back of the believer; whoever forbids what is wrong humbles the nose of the hypocrite; and whoever hates the hypocrites and becomes angry for the sake of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, Allah the Exalted becomes angry on his behalf."

Abu al-Darda' said: "You must enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or Allah will set over you a tyrannical ruler who will not honour your elder nor show mercy to your young; your best will supplicate but not be answered, they will seek victory but not be given it, and they will seek forgiveness but not be forgiven."

Hudhayfa al-Yamani said: "A time will come upon people when the carcass of a donkey among them will be dearer to them than a believer who enjoins them to do right and forbids them from wrong."

Al-Thawri said: "If a man is loved by his neighbours and praised by the people, know that he is a flatterer (mudahin)."

﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾, the verse [Al 'Imran 3:105]. Most exegetes (mufassirun) said: they are the Jews and Christians. Others said: they are the innovators (mubtadi'a) of this community.

'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad narrated: Abu Umama and I stood at the heads of the Harurites (al-Haruriyya, the early Kharijite group) in Syria, at the gate of Homs or Damascus. He said to them: "Dogs of the Fire, dogs of the Fire," twice or three times. "The worst of the slain, and the best of the slain are those they killed." [It was] said: "Is this from an opinion you hold, or something you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "If it were from an opinion I held, I would be very bold. I have not heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except once or twice—until he counted seven times—and I have not narrated it." A man said: "I saw your eyes filled with tears." He said: "It is a mercy that I had for them, for they were believers and then disbelieved after their faith." Then he recited ﴿And do not be like those who became divided﴾ up to ﴿after your faith﴾, and then said: "They are the Harurites."

Qabisa narrated from Jabir that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), when he arrived at a gate of Damascus called al-Jabiya, praised Allah and extolled Him as He deserves, then said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us as I stand among you, and said: 'Whoever desires the centre of Paradise should cling to the community, for Satan is with the lone one (al-fadh, the single individual), and from two he is further away.'"

﴿On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black, ...﴾: "a day" (يوم) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, meaning "on a day"; and the accusative of the time-expression here is by analogy with the object (التشبيه بالمفعول). Yahya ibn Wathhab read (تِبيض وتِسود) with a kasra on both taʼs, in the dialect of Tamim.

al-Zuhri read (تبياض وتسواد). As for those whose faces turned black...

The meaning: the faces of the believers become white and the faces of the disbelievers become black. It is also said: on the day when the faces of the sincere become white and the faces of the hypocrites become black.

'Ata said: the faces of the Emigrants and the Helpers become white, and the faces of Qurayza and al-Nadir become black.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: "On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black": he said: the faces of the People of the Sunna become white, and the faces of the People of Innovation become black.

al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: On the Day of Resurrection, for each people is raised what they used to worship, and each people go to what they used to worship, which is His saying ﴿We shall leave him to what he has turned to﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:115]. When they reach it, they grieve, and their faces turn black from grief. The People of the Qibla (Muslims), the Jews and the Christians remain, not knowing anything of what has been raised for them. Then Allah the Mighty and Majestic comes to them, and those who used to prostrate in worldly life, obedient and believing, prostrate to Him. The People of the Book and the hypocrites remain as if they cannot prostrate. Then they are permitted, and they raise their heads, and the faces of the believers are whiter than snow; and the hypocrites and the People of the Book stand as if there were spikes (al-safafid) in their backs. When they look at the faces of the believers and their whiteness, they grieve a severe grief and their faces turn black, and they say: "Our Lord, You have blackened the faces of those who worship other than You; so why are our faces blackened? By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists!" Allah says to the angels: "Look how they lied against themselves."

The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the whitening of faces is their brightness, joy, and delight in their deeds and Allah's reward; and their blackening is their grief, gloom, and dejection over their deeds and Allah's punishment. This is shown by His saying ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward] and more﴾ [Yunus 10:26], and His saying ﴿And those who earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is its like, and humiliation covers them﴾ [Yunus 10:27], and His saying ﴿Faces that day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:22], and ﴿faces that day will be overcast﴾ [al-Qiyama 75:24].

Then He explained their state and their end, saying: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?"﴾ There is an ellipsis here, meaning: it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve after your faith?" Scholars differed about it. al-Rabi' narrated from Abu al-'Aliya from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that they are everyone who disbelieved after his faith in Allah on the Day of the Covenant, when He brought them out from the loins of Adam (peace be upon him) and said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes﴾ [al-A'raf 7:172]. Allah the Mighty and Majestic will recognise them on the Day of Resurrection by their disbelief, and say: "Did you disbelieve after your faith on the Day of the Covenant?"

al-Hasan said: they are the hypocrites who gave the word of faith with their tongues, but denied it in their hearts and deeds.

Yunus ibn Abi Muslim said: I asked 'Ikrima about this verse, and he said: "If I were to explain it, I would not finish its explanation in three days; but I will summarise it for you. These are a people of the People of the Book who believed in their prophets and affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent; when he was sent, they disbelieved in him. That is His saying: 'Did you disbelieve after your faith?'"

Others said: they are from our religious community.

al-Harith al-A'war said: I heard 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) on the pulpit saying: "A man leaves his family and does not return to them until he has done a deed that merits Paradise; and a man leaves his family and does not return to them until he has done a deed that merits the Fire." Then he recited ﴿On the day when faces turn white and faces turn black...﴾ the verse.

Then "He called out to those who disbelieved after faith [Did you disbelieve?]" — evidence for this is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There will come upon my community a time when a man wakes up a believer and in the evening is a disbeliever, selling his religion for a small share of the world's goods."

Abu Umama al-Bahili said: they are the Kharijites (al-Khawarij). Qatada said: they are all the people of innovations.

The evidence for these interpretations is His saying ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against Allah, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar 39:60], and the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "There will surely be people from my companions who will be driven away from the Pool, until when I see them they will be pulled away from me, and I will say: 'My companions, my companions!' It will be said to me: 'You do not know what they innovated after you; they turned back on their heels.'"

﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾: these are the people of His obedience and the fulfilment of His covenant. ﴿Then in Allah's mercy﴾: the Garden of Allah. ﴿They will abide therein eternally﴾, up to ﴿and Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, that is, He does not punish them without guilt.

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned. You are the best community ever brought forth...﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:109–110]. Ikrima and Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning Ibn Mas'ud, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Mu'adh, and Salim the freed slave of Abu Hudhayfa, because Ibn al-Sayf and Wahb ibn Yahud, the two Jews, said to them: "Our religion is better than what you call us to, and we are better and more excellent than you." So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ refers to those who emigrated with the Prophet (ﷺ) to Medina. Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak: they are the Companions of Muhammad specifically, the transmitters and callers whom Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded to obey. This is supported by what al-Suddi narrated, that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said concerning ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "It applies to our first ones and does not apply to our later ones."

'Umar ibn al-Husayn narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Blessed is whoever sees me, and whoever sees one who saw me, and whoever sees one who saw one who saw one who saw one who saw me." [The manuscript repeats this phrase.]

al-A'mash narrated from Abu Salih from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile my Companions, for by Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Mount Uhud, he would not reach a mudd of one of them nor half of it."

Others said: they are the whole body of believers of this community. His saying ﴿you were﴾ means "you are," like His saying ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle a child?﴾ [Maryam 19:29], meaning "who is in the cradle." Inserting "kana" (was) and omitting it in such a sense has the same meaning, as in His saying ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-A'raf 7:86], and in another place ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [al-Anfal 8:26].

Muhammad ibn Jarir [al-Tabari] said: this is in the sense of completeness, and its interpretation is: "you were created and found to be the best community."

He also said: the meaning of ﴿you were the best community﴾ is with Allah in the Preserved Tablet. ﴿Brought forth for mankind﴾: some said: "for mankind" is connected to His saying "the best community," meaning: you are the best of mankind for mankind. Abu Hurayra said: its meaning is "you were the best of people for people, bringing them in chains and admitting them into Islam." Qatada said: they are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), to whom no prophet before him was commanded to fight; so they take captives from among the Romans, Turks, and non-Arabs and bring them into their religion. So they are "the best community brought forth for mankind."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: no other community among the followers of religions enjoins good and forbids evil towards the others and themselves, so that none of them wrongs another; rather they enjoin them to do right and forbid them from wrong. Therefore the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of the nations of mankind.

Others said: "for mankind" is connected to His saying "brought forth," and its meaning is: Allah has not brought forth for mankind a community better than the community of Muhammad (ﷺ); so they are the best community that has been established and brought forth for mankind. Reports have followed this interpretation.

Bahz ibn Hakim narrated from his father, from his grandfather, that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say concerning His saying ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾: "You will complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honoured by Allah the Mighty and Majestic."

'Abd Allah ibn Buraydah narrated from his father, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise are a hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them from this community."

Nafi' narrated from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no nation but that some of it is in the Fire and some in Paradise, but all of my community is in Paradise."

Thabit al-Bunani narrated from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The likeness of my community is like rain: one does not know whether its beginning is better or its end."

It is narrated from Anas, who said: A bishop (usquf) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and mentioned that he had seen in his dream the nations being prevented on the Bridge [.......] [an illegible word], until the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) came, radiant and with white marks. He said: "I said: 'Who are these, prophets?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Messengers?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Angels?' They said: 'No.' I said: 'Who are these?'"

They said: "The community of Muhammad (ﷺ), radiant with white marks, upon them the traces of ablution." When the bishop awoke, he embraced Islam.

It is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from 'Umar, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Paradise was forbidden to all the prophets until I enter it, and it was forbidden to the nations until my community enters it."

Abu Burda narrated from Abu Musa, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My community is a merciful community. On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will give every man of this community a man from among the disbelievers and say: 'This is your ransom from the Fire.'"

It is narrated from Anas, who said: I went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and suddenly a voice came from a ravine. He said: "O Anas, go and see what this voice is." I went and found a man praying towards a tree, saying: "O Allah, make me one of the merciful community of Muhammad, forgiven, whose supplications are answered, and whose repentance is accepted." I came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and informed him. He said: "Go and tell him: the Messenger of Allah sends you greetings and says: 'Who are you?'" I went to him and informed him of what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said. He said: "Convey my greetings to the Messenger of Allah and say: 'Your brother al-Khidr says: I ask [You] (أسألك) that You make me of your merciful community, forgiven, whose supplications are answered, and whose repentance is accepted.'" [A blank in the photographed manuscript; the apparent reading is what we have given.]

It was said to 'Isa (peace be upon him): "O Spirit of Allah, is there a community after this community?" He said: "Scholars, forbearing, wise, righteous, pious, as if they were prophets in knowledge; they are content with little provision from Allah, and Allah is content with little deed from them; He will admit them into Paradise by the testimony that there is no god but Allah."

We have been told that Ka'b al-Ahbar was asked: "Why did you not embrace Islam in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, but embraced it in the time of 'Umar?" He said: "Because my father gave me a sealed book and said: 'Do not break its seal.' Then during the days of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), I saw in a dream someone who said to me: 'Your father betrayed you concerning that document.' So I broke it, and in it was the description of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ): Salwoma, 'Alwoma, Hakuma, Safuha, and Kharuja." They asked him about its interpretation, and he said: "It means that their sign is that some of them greet others with peace; their scholars are like the prophets of the Children of Israel; Allah's judgment for them is Paradise; they shake hands, and they are forgiven and emerge from their sins as on the day their mothers bore them."

Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: This verse is a praise of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and He would not praise a people and then punish them.

Then He mentioned their virtues, saying: ﴿You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong﴾ up to ﴿they will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, the verse. Muqatil said: The chiefs of the Jews, Ka'b, 'Adi, al-Nu'man, Abu Rafi', Abu Yasir, Kinana and Abu Suriya, targeted their believers, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, harming them for their Islam. So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿They will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, meaning: they will not harm you, O believers, these Jews, except with hurt by the tongue, that is, threats and slander. It was also said: [it means] a call to misguidance. And it was said: a word of disbelief, which if they hear it from them, they will be hurt by it. ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you﴾ in flight, and this is a jussive (jazm) as the answer to the conditional, ﴿then they will not be helped﴾. He began a new clause [[i.e., made thumma (then) a resumptive (isti'nafiyya) particle, not a conjunctive one; had he made it conjunctive, the verb after it would be in the jussive.]] for the sake of the ends of verses, since they end in the nūn, like His saying ﴿and they will not be given leave, so they will not make excuses﴾ [[Al-Mursalat: 36.]]. Its implied sense is: then they will not be helped.

He said in another place: ﴿It will not be decreed for them so that they die﴾ [[Fatir: 36.]], since it was not the end of a verse.

The poet said:
"Have you not asked the old abode, so that it would speak?"
That is, so that it would speak [i.e., the fa' introduces the subjunctive, as it is governed by the verb].

Al-Akhfash said: His saying ﴿they will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾ is an exceptive clause (istithna') disconnected from the beginning of the speech, like the Arabs' saying: "He complains of nothing except good," and God, exalted is He, said ﴿They will not taste therein coolness or drink, except boiling water and dark pus﴾ [[Al-Naba': 24–25.]], and because this hurt does not harm them. Its meaning is: "but [they do cause] hurt."

﴿Humiliation has been decreed upon them wherever they are found﴾: wherever they are found and encountered, meaning: wherever they are met they are overcome, made weak, and killed, so they will not believe, ﴿except with a rope﴾: a covenant from God, ﴿and a rope from the people﴾: Muhammad and the believers, who return the tribute to them, and so they grant them security. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "unless they hold fast to a rope," like the poet's saying:
"She saw me with her ropes and turned away, out of fear,
and in the rope there is a frightened heart that trembles."
That is, she approached with her ropes.

Another said:
"The recurring days have bent me until
I seem like a crouching hunter approaching prey,
Near of step; whoever sees me thinks
I am not shackled, though I am in shackles."
That is: "whoever sees me" [is] "shackled [with a shackle]" [[In the manuscript: "for a shackle".]].

﴿They have incurred wrath from God﴾ up to ﴿They are not all alike﴾, the verse. Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil said: When 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Tha'laba ibn Sa'id, Usayd ibn Sa'id, Asad ibn 'Ubayd, and others of the Jews embraced Islam, the chiefs of the Jews said: "None believed in Muhammad except our wicked ones; if they had been among our best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers," and they said to them: "You have lost, since you have exchanged your religion for another." [[Ahkam al-Qur'an by al-Jassas: 2/45.]] So God, exalted is He, revealed ﴿They are not all alike﴾. "Alike" (sawa') requires two or more things. The scholars differed concerning the meaning of this verse. Some said: the speech contains an implied element, its meaning being: ﴿They are not alike [[As in the manuscript; there is a sign of omission over the word sawa', but no note on this omission is recorded in the margin of the manuscript's photograph.]] from among the People of the Book: a community standing [upright], and another that is not standing,﴾ so the other is omitted, because he mentioned one of the two groups, like the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:
"I disobeyed the heart in regard to her command,
though I am obedient to it; I do not know whether the guidance of her seekers
[is in her command] or error."
He meant: "whether it is guidance or error," and omitted it because the speech indicates it.

This is a collective, preceding statement, like their saying: "The mosquitoes bit me" and "Your companions went away." Others said: The complete statement ends at His saying ﴿They are not alike﴾, and this is a pause, because the mention of the two groups of the People of the Book has already occurred in His saying ﴿Among them are believers, and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Then He said ﴿They are not alike﴾, meaning the believers and the defiantly disobedient. Then He described the defiantly disobedient, saying ﴿They will not harm you except for a little hurt﴾, then He described the believers, saying ﴿a community standing﴾, the verse. So it refers back to the beginning of the speech, and this is the preference of Muhammad ibn Jarir [[Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/71.]] and al-Zajjaj. He said: "If you wish, you may make His saying ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾ the beginning of another statement, since the mention of the two groups has already occurred, then He said: 'These two groups are not alike,' and then began, saying: ﴿from among the People of the Book﴾."

Ibn Mas'ud said: its meaning is that the Jews and the community of Muhammad are not equal; the "standing" community is one that upholds the command of God, exalted is He, meaning one that is steadfast upon the upright truth. Ibn 'Abbas said: "a community standing" means guided, standing upon the command of God, not abandoning it as the others abandoned and neglected it. Mujahid: just. Al-Suddi: obedient, standing upon the Book of God, His obligations, and His limits. It was also said: standing in prayer. Al-Akhfash said: "a community standing" means possessing a standing community, and the "ummah" is a way, from their saying "amamtu al-shay'," meaning I aimed at it. Al-Nabigha said:
"Does one who possesses a path, while obedient, take counsel?"
That is, one who possesses a way.
The meaning of the verse is: two who have an upright way.

﴿They recite the signs of God﴾: they read the Book of God. Mujahid said: they follow, as it is said: "talahu," meaning he followed him. The poet said:
"You have made my bucket pour me down,
and I do not desire the follower of the companion..."
[Al-Sihah: 6/2273.]
"Indeed I did not desire them [...]" [[Two words not legible.]]
That is, you make me follow you.

﴿In the hours of the night﴾, that is, its hours, and its singular is "ini," like "nahi" and "anhaa'," and "ina" like "ma'a."
The poet said:
"Sweet and bitter, like the bending of an arrow is its disposition,
in every ini of the night's hours it puts on its shoes..." [[Lisan al-'Arab: 14/50, "ina".]]
That is, it entertains him in the hours of the night with a matter that passed and did not delay.
The rajiz in the other dialect said:
"By God, how excellent is Ja'far, what a youth,
girding up his leg in every ini."
Al-Suddi said: "hours of the night" means its middle.

Al-Awza'i related from Hassan 'Atiyya, who said: We were told that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Two rak'ahs that a servant performs in the middle of the night are better for him than the world and what is in it, and had it not been difficult for my community, I would have made them obligatory upon them." [106] [[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/368.]]

﴿And they prostrate﴾, that is, they pray, because recitation does not occur in bowing or prostration. Its parallel is His saying:
"And to Him they prostrate," that is, they pray. In the Qur'an: ﴿And when it is said to them, prostrate to the Most Merciful﴾ [[Al-Furqan: 60.]], that is, pray; and His saying ﴿So prostrate to God and worship﴾ [[Al-Najm: 62.]].

They differed concerning the revelation and meaning of the verse. Some said: it concerns the night prayer. From Majma' ibn Yahya al-Ansari, from a man of the Banu Shayba who used to study the books, who said: "We find a speech from the speech of [the Lord] [[In the manuscript: "the Arabs".]]: 'Does the herdsman of camels and sheep think, when night covers him and he is withdrawn, that he is standing and prostrating in the hours of the night?'"

Ibn Mas'ud said: it concerns the 'Atama prayer; they pray it while the People of the Book around them do not pray it.

'Asim, from Zirr, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) delayed the 'Isha' prayer, then went out to the mosque and found the people waiting for the prayer. He said: "Indeed there is no one among the religions who remembers God, mighty and majestic, at this hour except you." [107] [[Musnad Ahmad: 1/396; Asbab al-Nuzul of al-Wahidi: 79.]]
Then God revealed this verse: ﴿They are not alike﴾ up to His saying ﴿And God is Knowing of the God-fearing.﴾

Al-Thawri related from Mansur, who said: We were told that it was revealed concerning people who used to pray between Maghrib and 'Isha'.

'Ata said concerning His saying ﴿They are not alike. Among the People of the Book is a community standing﴾, the verse: it refers to forty men from the people of Najran of the Arabs, thirty-two from Abyssinia, and eight from Rum, who were upon the religion of 'Isa (peace be upon him) and affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ). Among the Ansar were a number of them before the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ), including As'ad ibn Zurara, al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur, Muhammad ibn Maslama, and Abu Qays Harma [[As in the manuscript.]] ibn Anas. They were monotheists, performing ritual washing from major impurity, and acknowledging what they knew of the laws of the Hanifiyya, until God, mighty and majestic, brought them the Prophet (ﷺ), so they affirmed him and supported him.

﴿And whatever good they do, they will not be denied it﴾. Al-A'mash, Hamza, Yahya, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read with the yā' in both places, as news about the upright community. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu 'Ubayda. The others read with the tā' in both places, in the address form, like His saying ﴿You were the best community﴾, and this is the choice of Abu Hatim. Abu 'Amr regarded both readings, the yā' and the tā', as valid.
