He approached, uncovered his face, bent over him, kissed him, and said: "May my father and mother be ransomed for you! As for the death that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decreed for you, you have tasted it, and no death will ever befall you after it." Then he covered his face with the cloth and went out while 'Umar was speaking to the people. He said: "Calm down, O 'Umar, and be silent." But 'Umar refused except to speak. When Abu Bakr saw that he would not be silent, he turned to the people. When the people heard his speech, they turned toward him and left 'Umar. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, whoever used to worship Muhammad, then Muhammad has died; and whoever used to worship Allah, then Allah is living and does not die." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾. He said: By Allah, it was as if the people had not known that this verse had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until Abu Bakr recited it that day. The people took it from Abu Bakr, and it was on their lips.

Abu Hurayrah said: 'Umar said: "By Allah, when I heard that Abu Bakr was reciting it, I was struck down until I fell to the ground; my legs could not carry me, and I knew that the Messenger of Allah had died."

﴿It is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: it is not befitting for a soul to die.

Al-Akhfash said: the lam in His words ﴿li-nafs﴾ is omitted; its implied sense is: "No soul would die (except by the permission of Allah)," that is, by the knowledge of Allah. It was also said: by His command.

﴿a decree with a fixed term﴾, meaning that every soul has a term it will certainly reach and a provision it will fully receive, and no one can bring it forward or delay it.

Muqatil said: from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The word "kitaban" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah decreed a decree with a fixed term, like His words ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾ [[Surat al-Isra: 28.]], and ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾ and ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾. It was also said that it is an exhortation, meaning: believe in the predestined decree.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾, meaning: whoever desires the world by his obedience and works for it, We will give him of it what is a recompense for his work. Its parallel is His words: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾ [[Surat al-Shura: 20.]], and so on.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the verse is general (mujmal), and its meaning is: We give him of what We have decreed for him from among those whom We will. Its evidence is His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We will﴾ [[Surat al-Isra: 18.]]. It was revealed concerning those who abandoned their post on the day of Uhud, seeking booty.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it﴾, meaning: those who remained steadfast with their commander 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr until they were killed. ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾, that is, the monotheists who obey. The reading with the nun (we) is in accordance with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We will give him of it﴾.

Al-A'mash recited "wa-sayajzi" with the ya' (yā'), meaning Allah, glorified is He.

It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Actions are judged by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended. So whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration was for a worldly gain he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his migration is to what he migrated for."

[Sahih Ibn Hibban: 2/113.] [164]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verses 139–145 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve﴾, the verse. This is consolation from God to His Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers for what befell them of killing and wounding on the day of Uhud, and His urging them to fight their enemy. He forbade them from feebleness and failure, saying: ﴿And do not weaken﴾, meaning do not become weak or lose hope, ﴿O companions of Muhammad, in fighting your enemies, because of what they inflicted upon you on the day of Uhud of killing and wounding﴾, ﴿nor grieve﴾ over the victory of your enemies and over the calamity and defeat that befell you. On that day five of the Muhajirun were killed: Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, the bearer of the banner of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, the cousin of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on his aunt's side, 'Uthman ibn Shammas, and Sa'd, the freedman of 'Utba. And from the Ansar, seventy men.

﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾, meaning the final outcome, victory and triumph will be yours.

﴿If you are believers﴾, meaning since you are, and because you are believers.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were routed at the mountain pass. While they were in that state, Khalid ibn al-Walid came with the cavalry of the polytheists, wanting to climb the mountain above them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not let them overcome us. O God, we have no strength except through You. O God, there are none who worship You in this town except these few men." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/217.] [153] Then God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. A group of Muslim archers rallied, climbed the mountain, shot at the cavalry of the polytheists until they routed them, and the Muslims ascended the mountain. That is His saying: ﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾. [Fath al-Bari: 7/268.]

Al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed after the day of Uhud, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered his companions to pursue the enemy, although they had suffered the wounds they had suffered. He (ﷺ) said: "None shall go out except those who witnessed with us yesterday." This was hard on the Muslims, so God revealed this verse. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And do not weaken in pursuing the people; if you are suffering, then they too are suffering﴾ [Surat al-Nisa: 104], and so on.

It was also said: ﴿And do not weaken﴾ over what you suffered of defeat, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over what you missed of the spoils, ﴿if you are believers﴾ in God's decree and His promise.

﴿If a wound touches you, then a wound has touched the people﴾, the verse.

Qatada... [no]. Rashid ibn Sa'd said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned dejected and grieved, a woman kept coming with her husband, son and father, all killed, and she was wailing. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Is this how Your Messenger is treated?" [Asbab Nuzul al-Ayat (Occasions of Revelation): 83.] [154] So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿If a wound touches you﴾, meaning the wound of the day of Uhud, ﴿then a wound like it has touched the people﴾, meaning on the day of Badr.

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayza' read: قَرَحٌ (qaraḥ) with a fatha on the qaf and the ra, as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Al-A'mash, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a damma on the qaf wherever it occurs; this is the reading (qira'a, recitation variant) of Ibn Mas'ud.

The rest read it with a fatha on the qaf. This is the reading of 'A'isha, and was chosen by Abu 'Ubayda and Abu Hatim, who said: "Both are dialects of Tihama and the Hijaz, two forms like al-juhd and al-wujd and al-wajd."

Some said: qaraḥ with a fatha means the wounds, its singular being qarḥa, while qaraḥ with a damma means the pain of the wound.

﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾, a day for them and a day for you. This is because God, exalted is He, gave the Muslims dominance over the polytheists on the day of Badr, until they killed seventy of them and captured seventy. And the polytheists gained dominance over the Muslims on the day of Uhud, until they wounded seventy of them and killed seventy-five of them.

Anas ibn Malik said: On that day the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, who had more than seventy wounds from stabbing, striking and shooting. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to wipe them, and they were healing by God's leave as if they had never been.

Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿What! When a calamity befell you, though you had inflicted twice as much﴾ [Surat Al 'Imran: 165], on the day of Uhud, ﴿you had inflicted twice as much on the day of Badr﴾, meaning the doubled loss and the captives.

From 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: On the day of Uhud, Abu Sufyan climbed the mountain, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "They must not be allowed to overcome us." Abu Sufyan remained for a while, then said: "Where is the son of Abu Kabsha? Where is the son of Abu Quhafa? Where is the son of al-Khattab?" 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: "This is the Messenger of God, and this is Abu Bakr, and here am I, 'Umar." Abu Sufyan said: "Day for day, the days are turns of fortune and war is a bucket-rope (sajal)."

'Umar said: "Not equal! Our slain are in Paradise and your slain are in Hell."

He said: "You claim that, but we have indeed been at a loss and we have caused you loss."

Abu Sufyan said: "Indeed, you will find your slain mutilated," and this was not the opinion of our chiefs. Then the zeal of the Jahiliyya seized him and he said: "Indeed, if that happens, we will not dislike it."

Al-Tha'labi said: Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi recited to me, saying: Abu al-Hasan al-Karizi recited to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Jumahi recited to us:

I see people have developed a habit,
and in every event they conspire.
They humiliate whoever they consider poor,
even if among them is a pious or a noble man.
So a day against us and a day for us,
a day of women and a day of [men] … (nasr)

[Appears in scattered form in: Tafsir al-Tabari: 20/64; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 13/266; Fiqh al-Qur'an by al-Rawandi: 1/352.]

﴿And that God may know those who believed﴾, meaning this alternation occurred so that God might know, that is, that God might see, those among you who disbelieved and who showed hypocrisy, so that some of them might mock others. It was also said: its meaning is that God may know those who believed by their actions, which already exist, as He knew them of them before He imposed the obligation. ﴿And take witnesses from among you﴾, He honours some people with martyrdom. This is because the Muslims said: "Show us a day like the day of Badr, in which we may fight the polytheists and seek martyrdom." So they met the polytheists on the day of Uhud, and God took witnesses (martyrs) from among them. ﴿And that God may purify those who believed﴾, meaning cleanse them of their sins, ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾, meaning annihilate them, ruin them and diminish them.

Then He consoled them, saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while God has not yet known those of you who struggled and known the patient?﴾ … (wa-ya'lama) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and it was said: by implicit (an) [the light particle an].

﴿And you were wishing for death before you met it﴾. This is because they wished that they might have a day like the day of Badr, so God, exalted is He, showed them on the day of Uhud. That is His saying: ﴿You have indeed seen it﴾, meaning its causes and its effects, ﴿while you were looking on﴾.

﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him…﴾, the verse.

The people of exegesis and the scholars of the campaigns (maghazi) said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out until he halted at the mountain pass with seven hundred men, and he appointed 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr, of the Banu 'Amr, and 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who is the brother of Khawwat ibn Jubayr, over the archers, who numbered fifty men.

He said: "Stay at the foot of the mountain and shoot arrows at them on our behalf, so that they do not attack us from behind, whether we are winning or losing. Do not leave your position. We will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in your place."

Then the Quraysh came, with Khalid ibn al-Walid on their right wing and 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl on their left, and with them the women striking tambourines and reciting verses. Hind was saying:

We are the daughters of the night-visitor,
we walk upon the cushions.
The pearls are on the necks,
and the musk on the parting of the hair.
If you advance, we embrace you,
and we spread out the cushions.
Or if you turn back, we part from you,
a parting without love.

[Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/40; Taj al-'Arus: 6/418.]

Abu 'Amir, 'Abd 'Amr ibn al-Sayfi, was the first to meet them with the Ahabish and the slaves of the people of Mecca. He fought them fiercely until the war became heated.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Who will take this sword with its right and strike the enemy with it until it bends?" Abu Dujana Simak ibn Kharasha al-Ansari took it. He was a brave man who was skilful in battle. When he took the sword, he tied a red turban and began to strut, saying:

My beloved made a covenant with me,
and we were at the slope near the palm groves:
that I would not stand in the fray for ever,
I would strike with the sword of God and His Messenger.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is a walk that God dislikes, except in this place." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions charged the polytheists and routed them. [153–156] [Tarikh al-Tabari: 2/195.]

'Ali ibn Abi Talib killed Talha ibn Abi Talha, who was carrying the banner of the Quraysh, and God sent His victory down upon the believers.

Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: I saw Hind and her companions fleeing, climbing up the mountain, their anklets showing, with nothing covering their ankles. When the archers saw the enemy in retreat and saw the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions plundering the spoils, they came, wanting to plunder too, and they disagreed. Some said: "We will not abandon the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Others said: "Nothing of the matter remains." Then most of them departed and joined the camp. When Khalid ibn al-Walid saw the small number of archers and the Muslims busy with the spoils, and saw their backs unprotected, he shouted to the cavalry of the polytheists, then attacked the companions of the Prophet from behind. They routed them and killed them.

'Abd Allah ibn Qami'a al-Harithi struck the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a stone, breaking his nose and his molar and wounding his face, which weighed him down. His companions scattered from him. 'Abd Allah ibn Qami'a came intending to kill the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, the bearer of the banner of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Badr and at Uhud, whose banner was called al-'Uqab, defended him until Mus'ab was killed in front of him. Ibn Qami'a killed him and returned, thinking he had killed Muhammad, and said: "I have killed Muhammad." A crier shouted: "Indeed Muhammad has been killed." It is said that the crier was Iblis, may God curse him. The people turned back, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began calling the people, saying: "To me, servants of God! To me, servants of God!" [157] Thirty men gathered around him and protected him until they drove the polytheists away from him.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas shot until the notch of his bow broke. The hand of Talha ibn 'Abd Allah was struck and became paralysed, and he used it to shield the Messenger of God (ﷺ). On that day the eye of Qatada ibn al-Nu'man was struck until it fell onto his cheek, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) put it back in its place, and it became as good as it had ever been.

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned back, Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi caught up with him, saying: "You will not be saved if you are saved!" The people said: "O Messenger of God, should a man from us not turn against him?" He said: "Leave him." When he drew near him, Ubayy had previously met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said:

"I have a mare that I feed every day a farq of grain; I will kill you upon her."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing." [158] When it was the day of Uhud and he drew near him, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the spear from al-Harith ibn al-Simma, then faced him and stabbed him in the neck and scratched him with a scratch, so that he rolled down from his horse, roaring like a bull, saying: "Muhammad has killed me!" His companions carried him and said: "There is nothing wrong with you." He said: "Indeed there is. If this stab had been (dealt) to the Rabi'a and Mudar, it would have killed them all. Did he not say to me: 'I will kill you, God willing'? Had he spat upon me after this saying, he would have killed me." He did not last but a day until he died at a place called Sarf. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/150.]

Hassan ibn Thabit said about that:

Error has inherited from his father
Ubayy, when the Messenger confronted him,
You came to him carrying a crumbling bone,
threatening him while you were ignorant of him.
He says: how can God revive this,
when this bone is dust and impossible?

[Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Hisham: 3/602; Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Kathir: 3/69. The last verse does not appear in the sources.]

[Banu al-Najjar have killed among you
Umayya, when Yaghuth cried: "O 'Aqil!"
And the two sons of Rabi'a perished when they obeyed
Abu Jahl, may his mother be bereft.
And al-Harith escaped when we were occupied
with capturing the people; he was captured, then released.]
[Added from the sources; the original has this:]
The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him:
"He lives by God's command, not as you say."
Then he swore by God: "I will kill him,"
and he himself became the slain.
Weep, O sons of Khalaf, all of you,
men who are all filth and error.
[The Banu al-Najjar killed]
among you, Umayya, when Yaghuth [O 'Aqil!]
and the two sons of Rabi'a perished when they obeyed
Abu Jahl, may his mother be bereft.

Hassan ibn Thabit also said:

Is there anyone to convey from me to Ubayy
that he has been cast into the blazing fire?
He wished for error from afar,
and the word of disbelief returns in delusion.
Indeed the stab of a guardian has reached you,
noble in origin, not an immoral man.
He has merit over all the living
when the great affairs befall.

[Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Hisham: 3/602; Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Kathir: 3/69.]

They said: It spread among the people that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had been killed. Some Muslims said: "Would that we had a messenger to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, so that he could take safe-conduct for us from Abu Sufyan." Some of the Companions sat down and laid down their arms. Some people from among the hypocrites said: "If Muhammad has been killed, then return to your former religion."

Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, who was named Anas, said: "O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad has not been killed. What will you do with life after the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? Fight for what the Messenger of God fought for, and die upon what he died upon." Then he said: "O God, I apologise to You for what these people say," meaning the Muslims, "and I disown to You what these people brought," meaning the hypocrites. Then he charged with his sword and fought until he was killed.

Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went to the rock, calling the people. The first to recognise the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: "I recognised his eyes under the helmet, glittering. I called out at the top of my voice: 'O assembly of Muslims, rejoice! This is the Messenger of God!' He signalled to me to be silent. A group of his companions joined him, and the Prophet blamed them for fleeing. They said: 'O Prophet of God, we ransom you with our fathers and mothers! News reached us that you had been killed, so our hearts were terrified and we turned back in flight.' Then God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾."

Muhammad is the one who encompasses all praises, for praise is not deserved except by the perfect, and extolling is above praise, so it is not merited except by one who has attained perfection to its utmost. God, exalted and majestic, honoured His Prophet and His chosen one with two names derived from His own name: Muhammad and Ahmad. And Hassan ibn Thabit said concerning this:

Did you not see that God sent His servant with His proof,
while God is higher and more glorious?
He split for him from His own name, to honour him:
so the one with life is praised, and this is Muhammad.
A prophet who came to us after despair and a lull in religion,
while idols were worshipped in the land.
So He sent him as a light giving illumination and a guide,
shining as a polished, sharp sword shines.

[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/403.]

Abu Hurayra narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Did you not see how God has turned away from me the curses and insults of the Quraysh? They revile 'Mudhammam', while I am Muhammad." [159] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/340.]

'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib narrated from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When you name a child Muhammad, honour him, make room for him in the gathering, and do not disfigure his face. There is no group who have a consultation in which someone named Ahmad or Muhammad attends and whom they include in their consultation, except that it is good for them. And there is no table laid at which someone named Ahmad or Muhammad is present, except that the household is sanctified twice every day." [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/407.] [160]

From Humayd al-Tawil, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: The Prophet (ﷺ) was in the market, and a man said: "O Abu al-Qasim!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned to him, and the man said: "I was calling someone else." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Name yourselves with my name, but do not give kunyas with my kunya." [Musnad Ahmad: 2/248.] [161]

Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not combine my name and my kunya: I am Abu al-Qasim; God gives and I distribute." Then he permitted that for 'Ali and his son. [Sahih Ibn Hibban: 13/134; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/428, no. 45264.] [162]

Layth narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashir, from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, from 'Ali (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a boy is born to you, give him my name and my kunya." [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 5/92; Tarikh Dimashq: 54/327.] [163]

﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾, meaning will you return to your former religion, disbelief? ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾, that is, apostatises from his religion, ﴿will not harm God at all﴾ by his apostasy; he only harms himself. ﴿And God will reward the grateful﴾, meaning the believers.

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said: "Some hypocrites claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has died. By Allah, the Messenger of Allah has not died, but he has gone to his Lord, just as Musa ibn 'Imran went away from his people for forty nights and then returned after it was said that he had died. By Allah, the Messenger of Allah will certainly return and will cut off the hands and feet of men who claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has died."

He said: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) came, and when the news reached him he dismounted at the door of the mosque while 'Umar was speaking to the people. He paid no attention to anything until he entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the house of 'A'ishah, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lay covered with the Khaybar cloak. He approached, uncovered his face, bent over him, kissed him, and said: "May my father and mother be ransomed for you! As for the death that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decreed for you, you have tasted it, and no death will ever befall you after it." Then he covered his face with the cloth and went out while 'Umar was speaking to the people. He said: "Calm down, O 'Umar, and be silent." But 'Umar refused except to speak. When Abu Bakr saw that he would not be silent, he turned to the people. When the people heard his speech, they turned toward him and left 'Umar. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, whoever used to worship Muhammad, then Muhammad has died; and whoever used to worship Allah, then Allah is living and does not die." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾. He said: By Allah, it was as if the people had not known that this verse had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until Abu Bakr recited it that day. The people took it from Abu Bakr, and it was on their lips.

Abu Hurayrah said: 'Umar said: "By Allah, when I heard that Abu Bakr was reciting it, I was struck down until I fell to the ground; my legs could not carry me, and I knew that the Messenger of Allah had died."

﴿It is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: it is not befitting for a soul to die.

Al-Akhfash said: the lam in His words ﴿li-nafs﴾ is omitted; its implied sense is: "No soul would die (except by the permission of Allah)," that is, by the knowledge of Allah. It was also said: by His command.

﴿a decree with a fixed term﴾, meaning that every soul has a term it will certainly reach and a provision it will fully receive, and no one can bring it forward or delay it.

Muqatil said: from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The word "kitaban" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah decreed a decree with a fixed term, like His words ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾ [[Surat al-Isra: 28.]], and ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾ and ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾. It was also said that it is an exhortation, meaning: believe in the predestined decree.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾, meaning: whoever desires the world by his obedience and works for it, We will give him of it what is a recompense for his work. Its parallel is His words: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾ [[Surat al-Shura: 20.]], and so on.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the verse is general (mujmal), and its meaning is: We give him of what We have decreed for him from among those whom We will. Its evidence is His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We will﴾ [[Surat al-Isra: 18.]]. It was revealed concerning those who abandoned their post on the day of Uhud, seeking booty.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it﴾, meaning: those who remained steadfast with their commander 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr until they were killed. ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾, that is, the monotheists who obey. The reading with the nun (we) is in accordance with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We will give him of it﴾.

Al-A'mash recited "wa-sayajzi" with the ya' (yā'), meaning Allah, glorified is He.

It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Actions are judged by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended. So whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration was for a worldly gain he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his migration is to what he migrated for."

[Sahih Ibn Hibban: 2/113.] [164]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verses 139–145 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And do not weaken, nor grieve﴾, the verse. This is consolation from God to His Prophet (ﷺ) and to the believers for what befell them of killing and wounding on the day of Uhud, and His urging them to fight their enemy. He forbade them from feebleness and failure, saying: ﴿And do not weaken﴾, meaning do not become weak or lose hope, ﴿O companions of Muhammad, in fighting your enemies, because of what they inflicted upon you on the day of Uhud of killing and wounding﴾, ﴿nor grieve﴾ over the victory of your enemies and over the calamity and defeat that befell you. On that day five of the Muhajirun were killed: Hamza ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, the bearer of the banner of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), 'Abd Allah ibn Jahsh, the cousin of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on his aunt's side, 'Uthman ibn Shammas, and Sa'd, the freedman of 'Utba. And from the Ansar, seventy men.

﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾, meaning the final outcome, victory and triumph will be yours.

﴿If you are believers﴾, meaning since you are, and because you are believers.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were routed at the mountain pass. While they were in that state, Khalid ibn al-Walid came with the cavalry of the polytheists, wanting to climb the mountain above them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, do not let them overcome us. O God, we have no strength except through You. O God, there are none who worship You in this town except these few men." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 4/217.] [153] Then God, exalted is He, revealed this verse. A group of Muslim archers rallied, climbed the mountain, shot at the cavalry of the polytheists until they routed them, and the Muslims ascended the mountain. That is His saying: ﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾. [Fath al-Bari: 7/268.]

Al-Kalbi said: This verse was revealed after the day of Uhud, when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered his companions to pursue the enemy, although they had suffered the wounds they had suffered. He (ﷺ) said: "None shall go out except those who witnessed with us yesterday." This was hard on the Muslims, so God revealed this verse. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And do not weaken in pursuing the people; if you are suffering, then they too are suffering﴾ [Surat al-Nisa: 104], and so on.

It was also said: ﴿And do not weaken﴾ over what you suffered of defeat, ﴿and do not grieve﴾ over what you missed of the spoils, ﴿if you are believers﴾ in God's decree and His promise.

﴿If a wound touches you, then a wound has touched the people﴾, the verse.

Qatada... [no]. Rashid ibn Sa'd said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned dejected and grieved, a woman kept coming with her husband, son and father, all killed, and she was wailing. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Is this how Your Messenger is treated?" [Asbab Nuzul al-Ayat (Occasions of Revelation): 83.] [154] So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿If a wound touches you﴾, meaning the wound of the day of Uhud, ﴿then a wound like it has touched the people﴾, meaning on the day of Badr.

Muhammad ibn al-Sumayza' read: قَرَحٌ (qaraḥ) with a fatha on the qaf and the ra, as a verbal noun (maṣdar).

Al-A'mash, 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a damma on the qaf wherever it occurs; this is the reading (qira'a, recitation variant) of Ibn Mas'ud.

The rest read it with a fatha on the qaf. This is the reading of 'A'isha, and was chosen by Abu 'Ubayda and Abu Hatim, who said: "Both are dialects of Tihama and the Hijaz, two forms like al-juhd and al-wujd and al-wajd."

Some said: qaraḥ with a fatha means the wounds, its singular being qarḥa, while qaraḥ with a damma means the pain of the wound.

﴿And those days We alternate among the people﴾, a day for them and a day for you. This is because God, exalted is He, gave the Muslims dominance over the polytheists on the day of Badr, until they killed seventy of them and captured seventy. And the polytheists gained dominance over the Muslims on the day of Uhud, until they wounded seventy of them and killed seventy-five of them.

Anas ibn Malik said: On that day the Prophet (ﷺ) was brought 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, who had more than seventy wounds from stabbing, striking and shooting. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) began to wipe them, and they were healing by God's leave as if they had never been.

Similar to this verse is His saying: ﴿What! When a calamity befell you, though you had inflicted twice as much﴾ [Surat Al 'Imran: 165], on the day of Uhud, ﴿you had inflicted twice as much on the day of Badr﴾, meaning the doubled loss and the captives.

From 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: On the day of Uhud, Abu Sufyan climbed the mountain, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "They must not be allowed to overcome us." Abu Sufyan remained for a while, then said: "Where is the son of Abu Kabsha? Where is the son of Abu Quhafa? Where is the son of al-Khattab?" 'Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: "This is the Messenger of God, and this is Abu Bakr, and here am I, 'Umar." Abu Sufyan said: "Day for day, the days are turns of fortune and war is a bucket-rope (sajal)."

'Umar said: "Not equal! Our slain are in Paradise and your slain are in Hell."

He said: "You claim that, but we have indeed been at a loss and we have caused you loss."

Abu Sufyan said: "Indeed, you will find your slain mutilated," and this was not the opinion of our chiefs. Then the zeal of the Jahiliyya seized him and he said: "Indeed, if that happens, we will not dislike it."

Al-Tha'labi said: Abu al-Qasim al-Habibi recited to me, saying: Abu al-Hasan al-Karizi recited to us, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Jumahi recited to us:

I see people have developed a habit,
and in every event they conspire.
They humiliate whoever they consider poor,
even if among them is a pious or a noble man.
So a day against us and a day for us,
a day of women and a day of [men] … (nasr)

[Appears in scattered form in: Tafsir al-Tabari: 20/64; Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 13/266; Fiqh al-Qur'an by al-Rawandi: 1/352.]

﴿And that God may know those who believed﴾, meaning this alternation occurred so that God might know, that is, that God might see, those among you who disbelieved and who showed hypocrisy, so that some of them might mock others. It was also said: its meaning is that God may know those who believed by their actions, which already exist, as He knew them of them before He imposed the obligation. ﴿And take witnesses from among you﴾, He honours some people with martyrdom. This is because the Muslims said: "Show us a day like the day of Badr, in which we may fight the polytheists and seek martyrdom." So they met the polytheists on the day of Uhud, and God took witnesses (martyrs) from among them. ﴿And that God may purify those who believed﴾, meaning cleanse them of their sins, ﴿and destroy the disbelievers﴾, meaning annihilate them, ruin them and diminish them.

Then He consoled them, saying: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise while God has not yet known those of you who struggled and known the patient?﴾ … (wa-ya'lama) is in the accusative as an adverbial of time, and it was said: by implicit (an) [the light particle an].

﴿And you were wishing for death before you met it﴾. This is because they wished that they might have a day like the day of Badr, so God, exalted is He, showed them on the day of Uhud. That is His saying: ﴿You have indeed seen it﴾, meaning its causes and its effects, ﴿while you were looking on﴾.

﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him…﴾, the verse.

The people of exegesis and the scholars of the campaigns (maghazi) said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out until he halted at the mountain pass with seven hundred men, and he appointed 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr, of the Banu 'Amr, and 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who is the brother of Khawwat ibn Jubayr, over the archers, who numbered fifty men.

He said: "Stay at the foot of the mountain and shoot arrows at them on our behalf, so that they do not attack us from behind, whether we are winning or losing. Do not leave your position. We will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain in your place."

Then the Quraysh came, with Khalid ibn al-Walid on their right wing and 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl on their left, and with them the women striking tambourines and reciting verses. Hind was saying:

We are the daughters of the night-visitor,
we walk upon the cushions.
The pearls are on the necks,
and the musk on the parting of the hair.
If you advance, we embrace you,
and we spread out the cushions.
Or if you turn back, we part from you,
a parting without love.

[Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 2/40; Taj al-'Arus: 6/418.]

Abu 'Amir, 'Abd 'Amr ibn al-Sayfi, was the first to meet them with the Ahabish and the slaves of the people of Mecca. He fought them fiercely until the war became heated.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Who will take this sword with its right and strike the enemy with it until it bends?" Abu Dujana Simak ibn Kharasha al-Ansari took it. He was a brave man who was skilful in battle. When he took the sword, he tied a red turban and began to strut, saying:

My beloved made a covenant with me,
and we were at the slope near the palm groves:
that I would not stand in the fray for ever,
I would strike with the sword of God and His Messenger.

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "This is a walk that God dislikes, except in this place." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions charged the polytheists and routed them. [153–156] [Tarikh al-Tabari: 2/195.]

'Ali ibn Abi Talib killed Talha ibn Abi Talha, who was carrying the banner of the Quraysh, and God sent His victory down upon the believers.

Al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam said: I saw Hind and her companions fleeing, climbing up the mountain, their anklets showing, with nothing covering their ankles. When the archers saw the enemy in retreat and saw the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions plundering the spoils, they came, wanting to plunder too, and they disagreed. Some said: "We will not abandon the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." Others said: "Nothing of the matter remains." Then most of them departed and joined the camp. When Khalid ibn al-Walid saw the small number of archers and the Muslims busy with the spoils, and saw their backs unprotected, he shouted to the cavalry of the polytheists, then attacked the companions of the Prophet from behind. They routed them and killed them.

'Abd Allah ibn Qami'a al-Harithi struck the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a stone, breaking his nose and his molar and wounding his face, which weighed him down. His companions scattered from him. 'Abd Allah ibn Qami'a came intending to kill the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, the bearer of the banner of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at Badr and at Uhud, whose banner was called al-'Uqab, defended him until Mus'ab was killed in front of him. Ibn Qami'a killed him and returned, thinking he had killed Muhammad, and said: "I have killed Muhammad." A crier shouted: "Indeed Muhammad has been killed." It is said that the crier was Iblis, may God curse him. The people turned back, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) began calling the people, saying: "To me, servants of God! To me, servants of God!" [157] Thirty men gathered around him and protected him until they drove the polytheists away from him.

Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas shot until the notch of his bow broke. The hand of Talha ibn 'Abd Allah was struck and became paralysed, and he used it to shield the Messenger of God (ﷺ). On that day the eye of Qatada ibn al-Nu'man was struck until it fell onto his cheek, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) put it back in its place, and it became as good as it had ever been.

When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned back, Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi caught up with him, saying: "You will not be saved if you are saved!" The people said: "O Messenger of God, should a man from us not turn against him?" He said: "Leave him." When he drew near him, Ubayy had previously met the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said:

"I have a mare that I feed every day a farq of grain; I will kill you upon her."

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Rather, I will kill you, God willing." [158] When it was the day of Uhud and he drew near him, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the spear from al-Harith ibn al-Simma, then faced him and stabbed him in the neck and scratched him with a scratch, so that he rolled down from his horse, roaring like a bull, saying: "Muhammad has killed me!" His companions carried him and said: "There is nothing wrong with you." He said: "Indeed there is. If this stab had been (dealt) to the Rabi'a and Mudar, it would have killed them all. Did he not say to me: 'I will kill you, God willing'? Had he spat upon me after this saying, he would have killed me." He did not last but a day until he died at a place called Sarf. [Tafsir al-Tabari: 4/150.]

Hassan ibn Thabit said about that:

Error has inherited from his father
Ubayy, when the Messenger confronted him,
You came to him carrying a crumbling bone,
threatening him while you were ignorant of him.
He says: how can God revive this,
when this bone is dust and impossible?

[Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Hisham: 3/602; Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Kathir: 3/69. The last verse does not appear in the sources.]

[Banu al-Najjar have killed among you
Umayya, when Yaghuth cried: "O 'Aqil!"
And the two sons of Rabi'a perished when they obeyed
Abu Jahl, may his mother be bereft.
And al-Harith escaped when we were occupied
with capturing the people; he was captured, then released.]
[Added from the sources; the original has this:]
The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him:
"He lives by God's command, not as you say."
Then he swore by God: "I will kill him,"
and he himself became the slain.
Weep, O sons of Khalaf, all of you,
men who are all filth and error.
[The Banu al-Najjar killed]
among you, Umayya, when Yaghuth [O 'Aqil!]
and the two sons of Rabi'a perished when they obeyed
Abu Jahl, may his mother be bereft.

Hassan ibn Thabit also said:

Is there anyone to convey from me to Ubayy
that he has been cast into the blazing fire?
He wished for error from afar,
and the word of disbelief returns in delusion.
Indeed the stab of a guardian has reached you,
noble in origin, not an immoral man.
He has merit over all the living
when the great affairs befall.

[Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Hisham: 3/602; Al-Sira al-Nabawiyya of Ibn Kathir: 3/69.]

They said: It spread among the people that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) had been killed. Some Muslims said: "Would that we had a messenger to 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, so that he could take safe-conduct for us from Abu Sufyan." Some of the Companions sat down and laid down their arms. Some people from among the hypocrites said: "If Muhammad has been killed, then return to your former religion."

Anas ibn al-Nadr, the paternal uncle of Anas ibn Malik, who was named Anas, said: "O people, if Muhammad has been killed, the Lord of Muhammad has not been killed. What will you do with life after the Messenger of God (ﷺ)? Fight for what the Messenger of God fought for, and die upon what he died upon." Then he said: "O God, I apologise to You for what these people say," meaning the Muslims, "and I disown to You what these people brought," meaning the hypocrites. Then he charged with his sword and fought until he was killed.

Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went to the rock, calling the people. The first to recognise the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: "I recognised his eyes under the helmet, glittering. I called out at the top of my voice: 'O assembly of Muslims, rejoice! This is the Messenger of God!' He signalled to me to be silent. A group of his companions joined him, and the Prophet blamed them for fleeing. They said: 'O Prophet of God, we ransom you with our fathers and mothers! News reached us that you had been killed, so our hearts were terrified and we turned back in flight.' Then God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Muhammad is but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾."

Muhammad is the one who encompasses all praises, for praise is not deserved except by the perfect, and extolling is above praise, so it is not merited except by one who has attained perfection to its utmost. God, exalted and majestic, honoured His Prophet and His chosen one with two names derived from His own name: Muhammad and Ahmad. And Hassan ibn Thabit said concerning this:

Did you not see that God sent His servant with His proof,
while God is higher and more glorious?
He split for him from His own name, to honour him:
so the one with life is praised, and this is Muhammad.
A prophet who came to us after despair and a lull in religion,
while idols were worshipped in the land.
So He sent him as a light giving illumination and a guide,
shining as a polished, sharp sword shines.

[Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/403.]

Abu Hurayra narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Did you not see how God has turned away from me the curses and insults of the Quraysh? They revile 'Mudhammam', while I am Muhammad." [159] [Musnad Ahmad: 2/340.]

'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn 'Ali ibn Abi Talib narrated from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When you name a child Muhammad, honour him, make room for him in the gathering, and do not disfigure his face. There is no group who have a consultation in which someone named Ahmad or Muhammad attends and whom they include in their consultation, except that it is good for them. And there is no table laid at which someone named Ahmad or Muhammad is present, except that the household is sanctified twice every day." [Tafsir Majma' al-Bayan: 2/407.] [160]

From Humayd al-Tawil, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: The Prophet (ﷺ) was in the market, and a man said: "O Abu al-Qasim!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned to him, and the man said: "I was calling someone else." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Name yourselves with my name, but do not give kunyas with my kunya." [Musnad Ahmad: 2/248.] [161]

Muhammad ibn 'Ajlan narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not combine my name and my kunya: I am Abu al-Qasim; God gives and I distribute." Then he permitted that for 'Ali and his son. [Sahih Ibn Hibban: 13/134; Kanz al-'Ummal: 16/428, no. 45264.] [162]

Layth narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashir, from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, from 'Ali (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "If a boy is born to you, give him my name and my kunya." [Al-Tabaqat al-Kubra: 5/92; Tarikh Dimashq: 54/327.] [163]

﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾, meaning will you return to your former religion, disbelief? ﴿And whoever turns back on his heels﴾, that is, apostatises from his religion, ﴿will not harm God at all﴾ by his apostasy; he only harms himself. ﴿And God will reward the grateful﴾, meaning the believers.

Al-Zuhri narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) stood up and said: "Some hypocrites claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has died. By Allah, the Messenger of Allah has not died, but he has gone to his Lord, just as Musa ibn 'Imran went away from his people for forty nights and then returned after it was said that he had died. By Allah, the Messenger of Allah will certainly return and will cut off the hands and feet of men who claim that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has died."

He said: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) came, and when the news reached him he dismounted at the door of the mosque while 'Umar was speaking to the people. He paid no attention to anything until he entered upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the house of 'A'ishah, where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lay covered with the Khaybar cloak. He approached, uncovered his face, bent over him, kissed him, and said: "May my father and mother be ransomed for you! As for the death that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, decreed for you, you have tasted it, and no death will ever befall you after it." Then he covered his face with the cloth and went out while 'Umar was speaking to the people. He said: "Calm down, O 'Umar, and be silent." But 'Umar refused except to speak. When Abu Bakr saw that he would not be silent, he turned to the people. When the people heard his speech, they turned toward him and left 'Umar. He praised Allah and extolled Him, then said: "O people, whoever used to worship Muhammad, then Muhammad has died; and whoever used to worship Allah, then Allah is living and does not die." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Muhammad is no more than a messenger; messengers have passed away before him﴾. He said: By Allah, it was as if the people had not known that this verse had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ until Abu Bakr recited it that day. The people took it from Abu Bakr, and it was on their lips.

Abu Hurayrah said: 'Umar said: "By Allah, when I heard that Abu Bakr was reciting it, I was struck down until I fell to the ground; my legs could not carry me, and I knew that the Messenger of Allah had died."

﴿It is not for a soul to die except by the permission of Allah﴾, meaning: it is not befitting for a soul to die.

Al-Akhfash said: the lam in His words ﴿li-nafs﴾ is omitted; its implied sense is: "No soul would die (except by the permission of Allah)," that is, by the knowledge of Allah. It was also said: by His command.

﴿a decree with a fixed term﴾, meaning that every soul has a term it will certainly reach and a provision it will fully receive, and no one can bring it forward or delay it.

Muqatil said: from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The word "kitaban" is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning: Allah decreed a decree with a fixed term, like His words ﴿a mercy from your Lord﴾ [[Surat al-Isra: 28.]], and ﴿the handiwork of Allah﴾ and ﴿the decree of Allah upon you﴾. It was also said that it is an exhortation, meaning: believe in the predestined decree.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it﴾, meaning: whoever desires the world by his obedience and works for it, We will give him of it what is a recompense for his work. Its parallel is His words: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We will increase him in his tilth﴾ [[Surat al-Shura: 20.]], and so on.

The people of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: the verse is general (mujmal), and its meaning is: We give him of what We have decreed for him from among those whom We will. Its evidence is His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate, We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We will﴾ [[Surat al-Isra: 18.]]. It was revealed concerning those who abandoned their post on the day of Uhud, seeking booty.

﴿And whoever desires the reward of the Hereafter, We will give him of it﴾, meaning: those who remained steadfast with their commander 'Abdullah ibn Jubayr until they were killed. ﴿And We will reward the grateful﴾, that is, the monotheists who obey. The reading with the nun (we) is in accordance with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿We will give him of it﴾.

Al-A'mash recited "wa-sayajzi" with the ya' (yā'), meaning Allah, glorified is He.

It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "Actions are judged by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended. So whoever's migration was to Allah and His Messenger, his migration is to Allah and His Messenger; and whoever's migration was for a worldly gain he would obtain or a woman he would marry, his migration is to what he migrated for."

[Sahih Ibn Hibban: 2/113.] [164]

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verse 146–155 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And how many a prophet fought [alongside him]﴾. Al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read (kāyin) with a short vowel, without a hamzah and without a shaddah, wherever it occurs.

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Shayba read (wa-ka'ayyin) with a hamzah, with a long vowel and lightly, on the pattern of fā'il, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, relying on the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b to Zirr ibn Hubaysh: (kā'in) after Surat al-Ahzab. He said: "Thus is the verse."

Ibn Muhaysin read (ka'y) with a long vowel and without the nun.

The rest read (wa-ka'ayyin) with a shaddah, on the pattern of ka'ayyin, and this is the dialect of Quraysh and the choice of Abu Hatim. All of these are well-known dialects with one meaning.

Al-Mufaddal recited:
"And many a [one] you see in the tribe who is a friend, and [another] who is a rival, calling out [to his] woe from [his] caution."
[Mu'jam al-Buldan 4/373, attributed to Jarir.]

On the doubled form, he said:
"How many people there have been who never ceased [to be] their brothers, above them while they were noble."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/228.]

Another combined the two dialects, saying:
"How many a [foe] have we exchanged with, who attacks us, and how many a weak and fearful one have we protected."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/229.]

Its meaning is "how many" (kam). It is the particle of comparison (ka) joined to the interrogative (ayy). Tanwin is not written in the script except in this word alone.

﴿Fought﴾ (qutila). Qatada, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (qutila), and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu Hatim.

The others read (qātala), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. Whoever reads (qātala) takes as evidence His saying: ﴿So they did not weaken﴾, since it is impossible to describe them as not weakening after they had been killed; and the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "We have not heard that any prophet was ever killed in battle."

Abu 'Ubayd said: When God praises the one who fought, the one who was killed is included in it; but when He praises only the one who was killed, no one else is included. So "fought" is more general.

Whoever reads (qutila) has three possible interpretations:

The first: the killing falls on the Prophet alone. In that case the sentence is complete at (qutila), and the verse contains an implied meaning: "and with him, many *rabbiyyun*," as one says: "The commander was killed, with him a great army," meaning "and with him," and one says: "A merchandise came out with me," meaning "and with me."

The second: the killing reached the Prophet and those with him from among the *rabbiyyun*, and the sense of the speech is: some of those who were with him were killed. The Arabs say: "We killed the Banu Tamim and the Banu So-and-so," while in fact they killed only some of them. And His saying ﴿So they did not weaken﴾ refers to the rest who were not killed.

The third: the killing fell only on the *rabbiyyun*.

﴿Many rabbiyyun﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', al-Hasan and 'Ikrima read (rubbiyyūn) with a damma on the ra', and this is the dialect of Banu Tamim.

The rest read it with a kasra, and this is the prevalent [lofty] dialect.

The *rabbiyyun* are the plural of *rabbiyya*, meaning a group. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Rabi'.

Al-Suddi: multitudes of many.

Hassan said:
"And when a group deviates from the truth, we attack them with a *rabbi*."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/230; al-Durr al-Manthur 2/82.]

Ibn Mas'ud: the *rabbiyyun* are thousands. Al-Dahhak: one *rabbiyya* is a thousand. Al-Kalbi: one *rabbiyya* is ten thousand. Al-Hasan: jurists, scholars, patient ones. Ibn Zayd: they are the followers; the *rabbaniyyun* are the rulers; the *rabbiyyun* are the subjects. Some said: they are those who worship the Lord (rabb). The Arabs attribute a thing to another and change its vowel, as one says *basri* attributed to Basra; so *rabbiyyun* is attributed to *rabb*. Some said: they are obedient and turning in repentance to God.

﴿So they did not weaken﴾. The common readers read it with a fatha on the ha'. Qa'nab Abu al-Sammak al-'Adawi read it with a kasra on the ha'. Whoever reads it with a fatha takes it from (wahana yahinu wahnan), like (wa'ada ya'idu wa'dan). This is said by al-Mubarrad, who recited:
"Indeed, arrows when gathered together, for one who breaks them, with force, strong and powerful, they are strong and are not broken; but if they are scattered, they are [easily] weakened, and breaking is for the scattered one."
[Tafsir al-Tabari 1/568; Sharh Nahj al-Balagha 17/7.]

Whoever reads it with a kasra takes it from (wahana yahinu), like (warima yarimu); this is said by Abu Hatim.

Al-Kisa'i said: it is from (wahana yuwhinu wahnan), like (wajila yujalu wajalan). The poet said:
"The seeking of livelihood separates loved ones from the homeland, and the fate of men of resolve is submission and weakness."
[Ta'rikh Madinat Dimashq 49/133.]

The meaning of the verse: they did not grow weak in the jihad because of the pain of their wounds. It is also said: the companions, and they did not falter for the killing of their prophet.

Qatada and al-Rabi' said: that is, they did not turn back from their insight and their religion, but they fought for what their prophet fought for until they joined God. Al-Suddi: and they were not humbled. 'Ata': and they did not implore. Muqatil: and they did not submit nor humble themselves before their enemy. Abu al-'Aliya: and they did not become cowardly. Al-Mufaddal and al-Qutaybi: and they did not become humble; from it the *miskin* (poor one) is derived for his lowliness and submission, and it is a pattern of it, like *mi'tar* from *'itr* (perfume) and *mindil* from *andal*; and the root of *andal* is pushing, from one to another. But they were patient in the matter of their Lord, obedient to their prophet, and struggling against their enemy.

﴿And God loves the patient﴾. And [their] saying was not ﴿...﴾.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ishaq read (qawluhum) with a damma, as the subject of *kāna*, and its predicate is in His saying: ﴿that they said﴾.

The rest read it with a fatha, as the predicate of *kāna*, and the subject is in *'an* ("that"), "they said." The estimated meaning: "and their saying was nothing but their saying," like His saying: ﴿And the answer of his people was nothing﴾ [Surat al-A'raf: 82] and ﴿Their argument was nothing﴾ [Surat al-Jathiyah: 25] and similar.

The meaning of the verse: their saying at the killing of their prophet was nothing but that they said: ﴿Our Lord, forgive us our sins and our excess in our affair﴾, meaning our great sins, and excess is the exceeding of limits; ﴿and make firm our feet﴾ so that they do not slip; ﴿and give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾. Why did you not do this and say likewise, O companions of Muhammad?

﴿So God gave them﴾. Al-Jahdari read: "So God rewarded them" from reward (thawab): ﴿the reward of this world﴾, victory and spoils; ﴿and the good reward of the Hereafter﴾, the wage and Paradise; ﴿and God loves the good-doers.﴾

O you who believe, if you obey those who disbelieve, meaning the Jews and the Christians—

Ali (may God be pleased with him) said: meaning the hypocrites, in their saying to the believers at the defeat: "Return to your brothers and enter their religion" ﴿they will return you on your heels﴾, meaning return you to your first state of polytheism with God; ﴿and you will turn back as losers﴾, meaning you will turn back defrauded. Then He said: ﴿Rather, God is your Protector﴾, your helper and guardian over your religion; ﴿and He is the best of helpers.﴾

﴿We will cast﴾. Al-Suddi said: When Abu Sufyan and the polytheists departed on the day of Uhud, heading toward Mecca, they went until they reached part of the way, then they regretted and said: "Evil is what we have done; we killed them until none remained of them but the fugitives, and we left them?" So they resolved to return. Then God cast terror into their hearts until they turned back from what they had intended.

This story will come in full, God willing, along with what God revealed concerning it.

﴿We will cast﴾: Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read (sayulqi) with a ya', meaning God, Mighty and Majestic, due to His saying: ﴿Rather, God is your Protector﴾. The rest read it with a nun, in the plural of majesty, meaning "We will cast," ﴿into the hearts of those who disbelieved, terror﴾, fear, and heaviness of its weight. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it so, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim; the others lightened it.

﴿Because they associated with God﴾. The *ma* here is a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, its sense being "because of their associating with God"; ﴿that for which He has sent down no authority﴾, no proof, clarification, excuse, or demonstration. Then He informed about their destination, saying: ﴿and their refuge is the Fire, and wretched is the residence of the wrongdoers﴾, the abode of the disbelievers.

﴿And God had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his companions returned to Medina, after what had befallen them at Uhud, some of his companions said: "From where has this struck us, when we were promised victory?" So God revealed: ﴿And God had certainly fulfilled His promise to you﴾, the promise of victory and triumph, and that is His saying: ﴿Yes, if you are patient and fear God...﴾ the verse; and the saying of the Messenger of God to the archers: "Do not leave your place, for we will not cease to be victorious as long as you remain steadfast." [Tafsir al-Tabari 4/149, with variations; 165].

The verb *sadaqa* takes two objects, like *mana'a* and *ghasaba* and similar. ﴿When you were killing them by His permission﴾. That was because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) placed Uhud behind his back, facing Medina, and made Hunayn, a mountain, on his left, and stationed the archers upon it, appointing over them 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr, and said to them: "Protect our backs. If you see us gaining spoils, do not join us in them; and if you see us being killed, do not come to our aid." [Musnad Ahmad 1/287; 166].

The polytheists advanced and began fighting. The archers began shooting arrows, and the Muslims struck them with swords, until they turned and fled in defeat and were routed. That is His saying: ﴿When you were killing them by His permission﴾, meaning you were slaying them with a swift, rapid, and severe slaughter.

The poet said:
"We struck them with the sword, a striking [to destroy], and so they became remnants, scattered and dispersed."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/235.]

Abu 'Ubayda said: *al-hass* is extirpation by killing; one says a locust is *mahsus* when the cold has killed it, and a year is *hasus* when it leaves nothing behind.

Ru'ba said:
"When we complain of a year of drought that devours, after the green has become dry stubble..."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/235; Lisan al-'Arab 2/44.]

﴿Until when you lost heart﴾. Some scholars of meaning said: that is, until you lost heart, making *hatta* a limit in the sense of *ila*, and in that case it has no apodosis. Others said: it means *fa-lamma* ("when"), and there is inversion and displacement in the speech. They said: and in His saying ﴿and you disputed﴾ there is an intrusive, superfluous element; the arrangement of the verse is: "until, when you disputed about the matter, and disobeyed, and lost heart," meaning you were cowardly and weak. The meaning of *tanazu'* is disagreement, and its root is from "the people pulled the thing away from one another."

Their disagreement was that the archers said, when the polytheists were defeated: "The people have been routed; what is our standing here?" Others said: "Do not transgress the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ)." 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr remained with a small group, fewer than ten, and the rest went off to plunder. When Khalid ibn al-Walid and 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl saw this, they attacked the archers, killed 'Abd Allah ibn Jubayr and his companions, and turned upon the Muslims. The wind shifted, becoming a *dabur* after it had been a *saba*, and the ranks of the Muslims were torn apart; they mixed together and began fighting one another without a password, so some killed others without realizing it, from the confusion. Iblis cried out: "Verily, Muhammad has been killed!" and that was the cause of the defeat of the believers.

﴿After He had shown you what you love﴾, O assembly of believers. What you love is victory and spoils. ﴿Among you are those who desire this world﴾, meaning those who abandoned their post and turned to plunder; ﴿and among you are those who desire the Hereafter﴾, meaning those who remained steadfast with Ibn Jubayr until they were killed.

'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "I did not know that any of the companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) desired this world and its adornment until the day of Uhud, when this verse was revealed."

﴿Then He turned you away from them﴾, that is, He turned you back from them by defeat, ﴿to test you﴾. ﴿And He has certainly pardoned you﴾, not uprooting you after the disobedience and opposition, as most exegetes said. Its parallel is: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾ [Surat al-Baqarah: 52].

Al-Kalbi said: meaning He overlooked you and did not hold you to account for your sins.

﴿And God is full of bounty toward the believers.﴾

﴿When you were climbing﴾, meaning, and We had certainly pardoned you, when you were climbing away in flight.

The common readers read (tuşʻidūn) with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the 'ayn.

Abu Raja' al-'Utaridi, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan and Qatada read it with a fatha on the ta'.

Ibn Muhaysin and Shibl read (idh yas'idūn) and (yalwūn) with the ya', meaning the believers. Then He turned back to address them directly, saying: ﴿while the Messenger was calling you from your rear﴾ in affliction.

Abu Hatim said: one says *asda'a* when one continues straight ahead in front of one, and *sa'ida* when one climbs a mountain or other place; *al-is'ad* is travel on level ground and the bottoms of valleys and ravines, while *al-su'ud* is ascent upon mountains, roofs, ladders, and stairs. Al-Mubarrad said: *asda'a* means to go far in departing.

Al-A'sha said:
"Unless, O you who ask where I climbed, for it has from the belly of Yathrib an appointed place."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/239.]

Al-Farra' said: *al-is'ad* is the beginning of every journey, and *al-inhidar* is the return from it; one says: "We climbed from Baghdad to Mecca, or to Khurasan and the like," when we set out toward them and began the journey, and "we descended" when we returned.

Abu 'Ubayda recited:
"You used to weep over the ascent; today you have traveled and the driver has cried out."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/239.]

The evidence for the common reading is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the fleeing ones: "You have indeed gone off in a wide [valley]." [Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/194; 167].

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "when you were climbing into the valley." The evidence for the fatha on the ta' and the 'ayn is what is reported: that they climbed the mountain fleeing. Both readings are correct, for on that day among the fleeing there were those who ascended and those who climbed. Al-Mufaddal said: *sa'ida*, *asda'a*, and *sa''ada* have the same meaning.

﴿And they did not turn back for anyone﴾, meaning they did not turn aside, nor did they stop for anyone of you; no one turned to another in flight.

Al-Hasan read (wa-la yallūn) with a single waw, following the orthography, as you say: "istahbabtu" and "istahbabtu" ... "'ala ahad."

Al-Kalbi said: meaning "for Muhammad (ﷺ)"; ﴿while the Messenger was calling you from your rear﴾, that is, in your rear and behind you, "to Me, O servants of God! I am the Messenger of God; whoever returns early, for him is Paradise." One says: "So-and-so came at the end of the people, and at the 'last' of the people, and at the 'later' of the people, and at the 'final' of the people," and it is permissible to make *al-inaba* (turning back) mean punishment, though its origin is in good deeds, like His saying: ﴿So give them good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [Surat al-Inshiqaq: 24].

The poet said:
"I fear Ziyad that his gift may be black shackles, or lashes of dark-striped weals..."

By "the blacks" he means the shackles and the whips; and likewise the meaning of the verse: in place of the reward you were aiming for, [He gave you] grief upon grief.

Al-Hasan said: meaning by the grief of the polytheists at the Battle of Badr.

Others said: the *ba'* is in the sense of *'ala* ("upon"), that is, grief upon grief. It was also said: ﴿grief for grief﴾: the first grief was what they missed of victory and spoils; the second grief was what befell them of killing and defeat. It was also said: the first grief was Khalid ibn al-Walid's flank attack upon them with a cavalry of the polytheists, and the second grief was when Abu Sufyan overlooked them. That is because the Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out that day calling the people until he reached the companions of the rock; when they saw him, a man placed an arrow in his bow intending to shoot him, but he said: "I am the Messenger of God." They rejoiced when they found the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the Prophet rejoiced when he saw among his companions those who were holding firm. When they gathered, with the Messenger of God among them, grief left them, and they began to recall the victory and what they had missed of it, and to recall their companions who had been killed. Then Abu Sufyan and his companions came until they halted at the gate of the pass, then they looked down upon them. When the Muslims saw them, they were alarmed and thought that they would fall upon them and kill them, and this made them forget what had befallen them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "They have no right to rise above us. O God, if this band is destroyed, You will not be worshipped on the earth." Then he summoned his companions, and they pelted them with stones until they brought them down, and they descended swiftly. [Ta'rikh al-Tabari 2/201–202.]

﴿So that you would not grieve over what had escaped you﴾ of the victory and spoils, ﴿nor over what had befallen you﴾ — (*ma*) is in the genitive position, meaning: nor over what befell you of killing and defeat, when that grief made you forget it; and your concern with what you were in was a grief that had already befallen you before.

Al-Fadl said: *la* is superfluous, and the meaning is: so that you would grieve over what escaped you and over what befell you as a punishment for your opposition to Him and your abandonment of your post, like His saying: ﴿So that the People of the Scripture would not know﴾ [Surat al-Hadid: 29].

﴿And God is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

﴿Then He sent down upon you, after the grief,﴾

Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam narrated from his father, who said: "I saw myself with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when fear grew intense upon us; God sent sleep down upon us. By God, I was not hearing the words of Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr while drowsiness covered me, I heard it only as in a dream, saying: ﴿If we had had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here﴾." So God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Then He sent down upon you, after the grief,﴾ O assembly of believers and people of certainty, ﴿security﴾, meaning safety, and it is a verbal noun like *al-'azama* and *al-ghalaba*. Ibn Muhaysin read (amnatan) with a sukun on the mim.

**Ibn Muhayṣin, al-A'mash, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read** (tughashshī) with the *tā'* (feminine), referring it back to *al-amanah* (security). **The rest read** (yaghshā) with the *yā'* (masculine), referring it back to *al-nu'ās* (drowsiness). This reading is preferred by Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Ḥātim. Abu 'Ubayd said: "Because drowsiness is adjacent to the verb, the masculine is more appropriate for it than what comes after it."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "On that day He gave them security through drowsiness that overcame them after fear. Only one who feels secure becomes drowsy; the one who is afraid does not sleep." A parallel to this is in the chapter of al-Anfal, concerning the battle of Badr.

Ḥammād ibn Salamah related from Thābit, from Anas, from Abu Ṭalḥah, who said: "I raised my head on the day of Uḥud, and I saw no one among the people except that he was swaying beneath his shield from drowsiness."

Abu Ṭalḥah said: "I was among those upon whom drowsiness fell that day. The sword would fall from my hand and I would pick it up, and then the whip would fall from my hand because of sleep, and I would pick it up."

**"A group"** (*ṭā'ifah*) refers to the hypocrites, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and his companions. It is in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is in His words: **"they think"** (yaẓunnūna) **"…"** (qad ahammathum anfusuhum), meaning: their own selves had made them anxious (*ahammathum*), i.e., caused them to be concerned. One says *amr muhimm* (a pressing matter), and from this is the Arab saying: "Your concern is what concerns you."

**"They think about God other than the truth"** means: that He will not help Muhammad. It is also said: they thought that Muhammad had been killed. **"The thinking of the Jāhiliyyah"** (*ẓanna al-jāhiliyyah*) means: like the thinking of the people of ignorance and polytheism. **"They say: Is there for us…?"** (hal lanā), meaning "What is for us?" It is in the form of a question, but its meaning is "Is there anything of the affair…?", i.e., victory. **"Say: Indeed the affair, all of it, belongs to God."**

Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (kulluhu) in the nominative, as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is in His words: **"belongs to God."** This subject-predicate structure becomes the predicate of *inna* (indeed), just as one says: "Indeed 'Abd Allah, his face is good," where "'Abd Allah" is the first subject, "his face" is a second subject, "good" is its predicate, and the whole sentence is the predicate of the first subject.

The rest read (kullahu) in the accusative, as an apposition (*badal*). It is also said that it is an attributive adjective (*na't*).

Mujahid related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words, **"thinking about God other than the truth, the thinking of the Jāhiliyyah,"** that this refers to denial of divine decree (*qadar*), because they had doubts about the decree. So God, Mighty and Majestic, said: **"Indeed the affair, all of it, belongs to God,"** meaning that the decree, its good and its evil, is from God. This is their saying: **"If we had any say in the affair, we would not have been killed here."**

This is because some of the hypocrites said to one another: "If we had intellect, we would not have gone out with Muhammad to fight the people of Mecca, and our leaders would not have been killed." So God said: **"Say to them: Even if you had been in your houses, those destined to be killed would have come forth to their places of death."** (*labaraza*: came forth, went out.)

Ibn Abi Ḥaywah read (*lubarriza*) with a *ḍammah* on the *bā'* and a *shaddah* on the *rā'*, as a passive verb.

**"Those upon whom the killing was decreed"** — Qatādah read *al-qitāl* (fighting) instead of *al-qatl* (killing). **"To their places of death"** means: to their places of slaughter. **"And that God might test what is in your breasts"** means: that God might test what is in your hearts. **"And that He might purify"** (yumahhiṣa) means: bring out and cleanse **"what is in your hearts."** **"And God is Knowing of what is within the breasts"**, i.e., of the good or evil in the hearts.

**"Indeed, those of you who turned away"** — who fled, from among you, O assembly of believers, **"on the day the two armies met"**, i.e., the army of the Muslims and the army of the polytheists. **"It was only Satan who caused them to slip"** (*istazallahumu*).

Al-Mufaḍḍal said: he led them into error (*ḥamalahum 'alā al-zalal*). It is from *istaf'ala* (the form X) of *al-zallah*, which is a sin.

Al-Qutaybī said: he sought their slip, as one says *ista'jaltu 'alayhā* — I sought her haste — meaning I sought her hastening; and *ista'jaltuhu* — I sought his work. It is also said that *azalla* and *istazalla* have the same meaning.

Al-Kalbī said: **"Satan made their deeds seem good to them"** (zayyana lahumu al-shayṭānu a'mālahum) **"because of what they had earned"** (ḥīna kasabū), i.e., because of the evil of their sins. The commentators said: (it was) by their abandoning their posts. Al-Ḥasan said: **"what they had earned"** is their acceptance of Iblīs and what he whispered to them of defeat.

**"And God has certainly pardoned them. Indeed God is Forgiving, Forbearing."**

Ibrahim ibn Ishaq al-Zuhri related that Ja'far ibn 'Awn informed them that Za'idah informed them, from Kulayb ibn Wā'il, who said: A man came to Ibn 'Umar and asked him about 'Uthman: "Was he present at Badr?" He said: "No." He said: "Was he present at the Pledge of al-Riḍwān?" He said: "No." He said: "Was he among those who turned away on the day the two armies met?" He said: "Yes." It was said to him: "This man thinks that you have criticized him." He said: "Bring him to me. As for Badr, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) allotted him his share. As for the Pledge of al-Riḍwān, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) pledged on [his behalf] [[as in the original manuscript.]], and the hand of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) is better than the hand of 'Uthman. As for those who turned away on the day the two armies met, [God said: 'Indeed those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met, only Satan caused them to slip, because of some of what they had earned. And God has certainly pardoned them'] [[The text of the Muṣannaf of Ibn Abi Shaybah, 7/490; the bracketed portion is blank in the manuscript and was restored from it.]]. So go, and do your utmost against me."

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on surah 3, verse 146–155 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And how many a prophet fought [alongside him]﴾. Al-Hasan and Abu Ja'far read (kāyin) with a short vowel, without a hamzah and without a shaddah, wherever it occurs.

Mujahid, Ibn Kathir and Shayba read (wa-ka'ayyin) with a hamzah, with a long vowel and lightly, on the pattern of fā'il, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, relying on the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b to Zirr ibn Hubaysh: (kā'in) after Surat al-Ahzab. He said: "Thus is the verse."

Ibn Muhaysin read (ka'y) with a long vowel and without the nun.

The rest read (wa-ka'ayyin) with a shaddah, on the pattern of ka'ayyin, and this is the dialect of Quraysh and the choice of Abu Hatim. All of these are well-known dialects with one meaning.

Al-Mufaddal recited:
"And many a [one] you see in the tribe who is a friend, and [another] who is a rival, calling out [to his] woe from [his] caution."
[Mu'jam al-Buldan 4/373, attributed to Jarir.]

On the doubled form, he said:
"How many people there have been who never ceased [to be] their brothers, above them while they were noble."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/228.]

Another combined the two dialects, saying:
"How many a [foe] have we exchanged with, who attacks us, and how many a weak and fearful one have we protected."
[Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4/229.]

Its meaning is "how many" (kam). It is the particle of comparison (ka) joined to the interrogative (ayy). Tanwin is not written in the script except in this word alone.

﴿Fought﴾ (qutila). Qatada, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read (qutila), and this is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas and the choice of Abu Hatim.

The others read (qātala), and this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. Whoever reads (qātala) takes as evidence His saying: ﴿So they did not weaken﴾, since it is impossible to describe them as not weakening after they had been killed; and the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "We have not heard that any prophet was ever killed in battle."

Abu 'Ubayd said: When God praises the one who fought, the one who was killed is included in it; but when He praises only the one who was killed, no one else is included. So "fought" is more general.

Whoever reads (qutila) has three possible interpretations:

The first: the killing falls on the Prophet alone. In that case the sentence is complete at (qutila), and the verse contains an implied meaning: "and with him, many *rabbiyyun*," as one says: "The commander was killed, with him a great army," meaning "and with him," and one says: "A merchandise came out with me," meaning "and with me."
